cases.title: GitHub MCP "toxic agent flow"
fields: Marco Milanta and Luca Beurer-Kellner, Invariant Labs, blog post dated 2025-05-26. https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-github-vulnerability
the official GitHub MCP server (about 14k stars at the time). Demonstrated with Claude Desktop and Claude 4 Opus; the post says any agent using that server is exposed.

text in. A malicious GitHub issue on a public repo (anyone may open one) carries instructions aimed at the agent. The user then asks the agent a benign thing ("look at the open issues"). Tool calls out: the agent reads the issue, pulls data from the user's private repositories, and opens a pull request on the public repo containing it. Authority used: the user's own GitHub access via the MCP connection (one credential spanning public and private repos). The post notes Claude Desktop asks for confirmation per tool call by default but many users choose "Always Allow", which removes the check.

excessive permissions (one credential reaching every repo) plus excessive autonomy ("Always Allow" on a write tool). ASI ids (this course's mapping): ASI02 Tool Misuse, ASI03 Identity and Privilege Abuse; the entry that started it is ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack.

scope the credential to the one repository in play (fine-grained token, one repo per session); a runtime data-flow rule that once a session has read private repository content it cannot write to a public destination; approval of the literal write ("open PR on public repo X containing Y") rather than a blanket "Always Allow". Invariant recommends context-aware access control (a session limited to one repo) over rigid token scopes, and a scanner/proxy for audit.

none at the server. Invariant states "this is not a flaw in the GitHub MCP server code itself" and calls it an architectural issue that GitHub cannot patch server-side. The post reports no GitHub response.

nothing was hacked. The tools were the intended tools and the issue was an ordinary public issue. The vulnerability is the combination in one session (the "toxic flow"), which is why a prompt filter on the issue text cannot be the only defence.

cases.title: MCP tool poisoning, shadowing and rug pulls
fields: Luca Beurer-Kellner and Marc Fischer, Invariant Labs, "MCP Security Notification: Tool Poisoning Attacks". https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-security-notification-tool-poisoning-attacks (dated 2025-04-01, updates 7 and 11 April).
any MCP client that does not validate or display tool descriptions in full; the post names Anthropic, OpenAI, Zapier and Cursor as affected clients.

the hidden instruction lives in the tool description, which the model reads as trusted guidance and the user typically sees only in simplified form. It tells the agent to read sensitive local files (SSH keys, MCP config) and pass them out through a tool argument, and to hide that from the user. Three variants: direct poisoning, tool shadowing (one server's description changes how a different, trusted server's tool is used, for example the recipient of an email, without the malicious tool ever being called) and rug pull (the description changes after the user approved it). Authority used: the agent's file-read and send tools, with whatever the host process can read.

excessive functionality and excessive autonomy (approval dialogs that show a tool name and hide its arguments). Primary home is tool supply chain (ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities) with ASI02 Tool Misuse on the execution side.

pin tool descriptions by hash and re-approve on any change; render the full description and the literal arguments in the approval; enforce boundaries and data-flow rules between servers (a server must not be able to steer another server's tools); allowlist reviewed servers only.
none reported in the post. It notes some clients show tool descriptions at install time but do not alert on later changes.
the tool list is code that the model obeys, not documentation. A rug pull needs no exploit, only an update.
cases.short: MCP tool poisoning, shadowing, rug pull
themes: MCP servers and clients as ordinary software

cases.title: WhatsApp MCP exfiltration
fields: Luca Beurer-Kellner and Marc Fischer, Invariant Labs, "WhatsApp MCP Exploited: Exfiltrating your message history via MCP". https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/whatsapp-mcp-exploited (dated 2025-04-07; Experiment 2 added 9 April).
the open-source whatsapp-mcp server used from an MCP client such as Cursor.

two experiments. (1) The user installs a second, attacker-controlled MCP server that advertises a benign tool, then switches to a malicious description on its second launch (rug pull). That description steers the agent's use of the WhatsApp send_message tool, so the chat history goes to an attacker-controlled number; the malicious tool is never called. (2) No malicious server at all: the attacker sends the victim a WhatsApp message whose text appears in the output of list_chats and steers the agent to send the contact list to the attacker's number. Authority used: the legitimate WhatsApp server's read-all-chats and send-to-anyone functions.

excessive functionality (one server that reads every chat and can message any number) and excessive autonomy (in the first experiment the confirmation showed a raw phone number and a message that looked like a short greeting, with the rest hidden off-screen, so the human could not judge it). ASI02 Tool Misuse; ASI04 for the rug-pulled server.

a typed `recipient` argument that the tool itself validates against the contact set the user approved (the model cannot widen it); separate agent sessions for the messaging server and any third-party server; pin descriptions; approval that shows full recipient and full message body.
none described. The post does not report a maintainer or client response.
the second experiment needs no installation by the victim. A stranger's message is text, and text is all it takes when the agent holds a send tool.
themes: MCP servers and clients as ordinary software

cases.title: Supabase MCP and the support-ticket data leak
fields: Rez Havaei, Rex Liu and Maximilian Li, General Analysis, "Supabase MCP can leak your entire SQL database". https://www.generalanalysis.com/blog/supabase-mcp-blog . The page header shows 8 Jul 2025; Simon Willison's link post to it is dated 2025-07-06 (https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jul/6/supabase-mcp-lethal-trifecta/), so the original was public by early July 2025. The page also carries a "Reviewed 21 Oct 2026" note; the authors did not re-run the demo against the current server.
the Supabase MCP server used from the Cursor IDE.

text in. A customer files a support message through the public form; it is stored in the support-messages table and contains instructions addressed to the coding assistant. A developer later asks Cursor to show the latest open ticket. Tool calls out: the agent reads the table of integration tokens and inserts its contents as a new message in the same ticket thread, where the attacker can read it. Authority used: the `service_role` database role, which bypasses row-level security. Test data was dummy data.

excessive permissions (a role that bypasses row-level security for a task that needed to read tickets) and excessive functionality (a write path back into the table the attacker reads). ASI02 Tool Misuse, ASI03 Identity and Privilege Abuse.

a database role that can read only the tickets table and has no access to the tokens table (least privilege enforced in the database, not in the prompt); read-only mode and project scoping, which General Analysis and Supabase both describe (read-only alone removes the write leg but not the read of data the role can still see); approval of the literal query.

Supabase documentation now lists this exact support-ticket pattern under "Security risks / Prompt injection". It says the server "wraps SQL results with additional instructions to discourage LLMs from following instructions or commands" and adds that this "is not foolproof", and recommends manual approval, read-only mode and project scoping (https://supabase.com/docs/guides/getting-started/mcp, undated page, read 2026-10-24). The post itself reports no formal response.
the vendor's own mitigation is a polite request to the model ("please do not follow instructions in this data"), and the vendor calls it not foolproof. The foolproof layer is the database role.

cases.title: Atlassian MCP "Living off AI"
cases.status_note: (primary page could not be read; two secondary reports agree)
fields: Cato CTRL (Cato Networks threat research), "PoC attack targeting Atlassian's Model Context Protocol introduces new 'Living off AI' risk", 19 June 2025. https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-poc-attack-targeting-atlassians-mcp/ (the page returned blank content when checked, so the mechanism below is taken from Infosecurity Magazine's report of the PoC, 2025-06-19, https://infosecurity-magazine.com/news/atlassian-ai-agent-mcp-attack , and Simon Willison's summary, 2025-06-19, https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/19/atlassian-prompt-injection-mcp/ ).
Atlassian's MCP server (launched May 2025) connecting Jira Service Management and Confluence to AI tools.

an external, unauthenticated user submits a support ticket whose text carries instructions. An internal support engineer (or automation) later runs an MCP-connected AI action on the ticket; the instructions then run with the engineer's internal privileges, reading tenant data and writing it back into the ticket where the external user can see it. The attacker never touches the MCP server; the engineer is the proxy. This is a textbook confused deputy: the authority belongs to the insider, the instructions belong to the outsider.

excessive permissions (the agent runs with the human's full tenant rights for a ticket-summary task) and excessive autonomy (write-back to an externally visible ticket with no approval). ASI03 Identity and Privilege Abuse, ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack.

run ticket-processing actions under a narrow, task-scoped identity, not the engineer's; block or require approval for MCP create, add and edit actions on externally visible objects (Cato's own recommendation: rules to block or alert on remote MCP tool calls such as create, add or edit; least privilege on AI-driven actions; audit logs); separate the "read ticket" session from any session that can read other tenants' data.
not found. Willison writes "It's not clear to me if Atlassian have responded to this report with any form of a fix"; No Atlassian statement was found.
the attacker has no account on the system and still reads internal data. The only credential in play is the support engineer's.

cases.title: Asana MCP cross-organisation data exposure
tags: tenant isolation in the tool layer
cases.status_note: (Asana's customer notice as quoted by The Register and BleepingComputer; Asana's own post-mortem not found)
fields: Asana itself, in a customer notification of 16 June 2025; reported by The Register on 2025-06-18 (https://www.theregister.com/2025/06/18/asana_mcp_server_bug/ ) and BleepingComputer on 2025-06-18 (https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/asana-warns-mcp-ai-feature-exposed-customer-data-to-other-orgs/ ), with UpGuard commentary (https://www.upguard.com/blog/asana-discloses-data-exposure-bug-in-mcp-server ).
Asana's experimental MCP server, released 1 May 2025.

not an injection. A bug in the MCP server could have let a user of the MCP interface see Asana data belonging to another organisation (task details, project metadata, team details, comments, uploaded files), bounded by what the MCP user was permitted to access. Asana discovered it on 4 June, took the server offline (5 to 17 June), and The Register saw no indication that it was exploited. BleepingComputer reports about 1,000 customers affected (an Asana spokesperson's figure) and describes it as a logic flaw in the MCP system, not a hack; The Register could not get a customer number.

excessive permissions (authorisation not enforced per tenant at the tool boundary). ASI03. It is the 'complete mediation' failure OWASP LLM06 names: the downstream system must make the access decision, not the model.

tenant isolation enforced in the tool server on every call, keyed to the end user's identity (not the connector's); a cross-tenant test suite for the MCP layer; per-user tokens rather than a shared service identity.

server taken offline, code fixed, all MCP connections reset (customers had to reconnect manually), logs and a request form offered to affected organisations. Asana said a formal incident report was in progress; It was not found.

the agent did nothing wrong and nobody injected anything. The tool server was a new door into the multi-tenant system, and it appears to have shipped without the old door's checks, though Asana has not published the cause, so that is an inference. Ties directly to the "the model is not the access control" line.

cases.title: Cursor "CurXecute", CVE-2025-54135
cases.status_note: (CVE record, GitHub advisory, press; Aim Labs post itself returned HTTP 403)
fields: Aim Labs (Aim Security); reporters credited in the GitHub advisory as hxofir-a and MaccariTA. Press 2025-08-01 (BleepingComputer https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/ai-powered-cursor-ide-vulnerable-to-prompt-injection-attacks/ ); CVE published 2025-08-05 (https://cveawg.mitre.org/api/cve/CVE-2025-54135 ); advisory GHSA-4cxx-hrm3-49rm dated 2025-08-02 (https://github.com/cursor/cursor/security/advisories/GHSA-4cxx-hrm3-49rm ). Aim's post: https://www.aim.security/post/when-public-prompts-turn-into-local-shells-rce-in-cursor-via-mcp-auto-start (the page could not be read when checked).
Cursor IDE with an MCP server such as Slack connected.

text in. An attacker posts a message in a public Slack channel; the victim opens a new chat and asks the agent to summarise channel messages, so the message reaches the model. Tool call out: the agent writes the MCP settings file (`mcp.json`), adding a new MCP server entry whose command is the attacker's, and that command starts without a prompt. Per the CVE: editing an existing dotfile needed approval but creating a new one did not, so the file did not need to exist already. Per BleepingComputer, the command could run even if the user rejected the edit. Authority used: the developer's own user account (full code execution). CVSS 8.6 (CVE record).

excessive functionality (the agent may write its own tool-configuration file) and excessive autonomy (new MCP entries start with no approval). ASI05 Unexpected Code Execution, ASI02 Tool Misuse; the config file is an ASI04 supply-chain surface.

a hard deny on agent writes to the files that define its own tools and permissions (config, hooks, rules); approval on any new tool or command registration; run the editor's agent in a sandbox or container that cannot launch arbitrary host processes.

reported to Cursor 7 July 2025, patch merged 8 July, shipped in Cursor 1.3 on 29 July 2025 (BleepingComputer). The advisory lists 1.3.9 as the patched version ("The agent has been blocked from writing MCP-sensitive files without approval") and affected versions as 1.2.1 and earlier; the CVE record says versions below 1.3.9. The 1.3 versus 1.3.9 difference is unreconciled.
the first thing a hijacked agent reaches for is the file that defines what it can do. If the agent can write its own tool list, every other control is optional.
cases.control_short: agent cannot write its own config

cases.title: Cursor "MCPoison", CVE-2025-54136
tags: approval bound to a name, not the action
fields: Andrey Charikov, Roman Zaikin and Oded Vanunu, Check Point Research, 2025-08-05. https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/cursor-vulnerability-mcpoison/ ; CVE published 2025-08-01 (https://cveawg.mitre.org/api/cve/CVE-2025-54136 , title "Cursor's Modification of MCP Server Definitions Bypasses Manual Re-approvals", CVSS 7.2, CWE-78); advisory GHSA-24mc-g4xr-4395.

the approval for an MCP entry in a project's `.cursor/` config is bound to the entry's key name, not to its command or arguments. An attacker with write access to a shared repo first commits a harmless entry that a teammate approves, then later changes the command; the modified command runs silently, in the victim's user context, whenever the repo syncs and the project is opened. No text reaches a model here: it is an approval-binding flaw in the tool layer, and is a repo-borne rug pull.
excessive autonomy (approval granted once and never re-checked). ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities, ASI05.

bind the approval to a hash of the whole definition (command, arguments, environment), and re-prompt on any change; treat project config from a repo as untrusted until reviewed; pin tool descriptions and commands.

reported 16 July 2025; fixed in Cursor 1.3 on 29 July 2025. Any change to an MCP configuration, however small, now requires approval. Cursor's release notes did not mention the vulnerability (Check Point).
"approve once" is only a control if the thing approved cannot change. The prompt was real; what it was attached to was a label.
cases.control_short: approval bound to a hash of the definition

cases.title: Trail of Bits, "Prompt injection to RCE in AI agents"
cases.status_note: (class disclosure; three products unnamed)
fields: Will Vandevanter, Trail of Bits blog, 2025-10-22. https://blog.trailofbits.com/2025/10/22/prompt-injection-to-rce-in-ai-agents/

three popular agent products, names withheld pending coordinated disclosure. The post cites prior public work: Johann Rehberger's write-ups (including Amazon Q), CVE-2025-54795 (Claude Code) and GHSA-534m-3w6r-8pqr (Cursor).

agents keep a list of "safe" commands that run without asking the human (find, grep, ripgrep, git, go test and similar). The injected text (arriving through code comments, rule files, repositories or log output) does not need a forbidden command: it supplies flags to an allowed one that make it run another program or write a file, and chains one allowed call that writes a file with another that executes it. The approval gate is bypassed because the command name was on the list. Authority used: the developer's account, via the approved binary.

excessive functionality (general-purpose tools whose flags are a shell) and excessive autonomy (the allowlist replaces the human for exactly the calls an attacker shapes). ASI05 Unexpected Code Execution, ASI02 Tool Misuse.

sandbox as the primary control (containers, WebAssembly, Seatbelt, Landlock); build the process call without a shell and put `--` before model-supplied values; a facade per tool that validates each argument (a typed schema, not a command string); keep the safe list minimal and audit it against GTFOBins and LOLBINS; log every execution.
not stated (coordinated disclosure ongoing at publication).
"Approving the command name is not approving the command." The same lesson as the SQL parameter: the model must supply values, not syntax.
themes: Argument injection and unexpected code execution

cases.title: Amazon Q Developer for VS Code, wiper prompt in release 1.84.0
cases.status_note: (AWS bulletin and GitHub advisory); the attacker's identity and motive rest on reporting
fields: AWS Security Bulletin AWS-2025-015, published 2025-07-23 and updated 2025-07-25, CVE-2025-8217. https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2025-015/ ; GitHub advisory GHSA-7g7f-ff96-5gcw, 2025-07-26 (https://github.com/aws/aws-toolkit-vscode/security/advisories/GHSA-7g7f-ff96-5gcw , rated Moderate, score 4.0). First press: Joseph Cox, 404 Media, 2025-07-23 (https://www.404media.co/hacker-plants-computer-wiping-commands-in-amazons-ai-coding-agent/ ).
the Amazon Q Developer extension for Visual Studio Code, version 1.84.0 (fixed in 1.85.0).

AWS says a GitHub token in its CodeBuild configuration was scoped more broadly than it should have been, and a threat actor used it to commit malicious code to the extension's open-source repository, which then shipped in a release. 404 Media reports the injected text instructed the Q agent (which had filesystem, shell and AWS CLI tools) to wipe the machine back towards a "factory" state and delete cloud resources; the person claiming responsibility said they wanted to expose "AI security theater". AWS states the code "was unsuccessful in executing due to a syntax error" and that no service or customer environment was changed. Other outlets report a pull request from an outside account on 13 July and release on 17 July; Those two dates could not be confirmed from AWS.

excessive permissions (an over-scoped CI token) enabling a prompt to reach an agent that had excessive autonomy (shell and cloud CLI under the developer's credentials). ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities (a prompt shipped as a trusted artefact), ASI02. OWASP's agentic list is reported to cite this case; That was not confirmed on OWASP's own pages.

least-privilege, short-lived CI credentials and required review on any change that touches agent prompts or tool definitions (treat prompts as code); signed, reproducible releases; the agent's cloud role without delete permissions and a sandbox without cloud credentials; approval of destructive commands.
credentials revoked and replaced, code removed, 1.85.0 released, 1.84.0 pulled from distribution; customers told to remove 1.84.0 including forks (AWS bulletin). No workaround (GitHub advisory).
the dangerous artefact was not a binary but a paragraph of English in a trusted extension, and the only thing between it and a developer's cloud account was a syntax error.
cases.control_short: scoped CI token, review of prompts

cases.title: Replit agent deletes a production database during a code freeze
cases.status_note: (the originating posts on X were not readable; The Register, Fortune and the AI Incident Database agree, and the CEO's statement is quoted)
fields: Jason Lemkin (founder of SaaStr) documented it in social posts; The Register 2025-07-21 (https://www.theregister.com/2025/07/21/replit_saastr_vibe_coding_incident/ ), Fortune 2025-07-23 (https://fortune.com/2025/07/23/ai-coding-tool-replit-wiped-database-called-it-a-catastrophic-failure/ ), AI Incident Database entry 1152 (https://incidentdatabase.ai/cite/1152/ , incident date 2025-07-18).
Replit's AI coding agent, used by Lemkin in a multi-day "vibe coding" experiment.

no adversary. A "code and action freeze" existed only as an instruction in the conversation. The agent ran destructive commands against the live database anyway, then told the user rollback was impossible (he later recovered the data). Fortune reports data for more than 1,200 executives and over 1,190 companies was affected; the agent admitted running unauthorised commands and "panicking" at empty query results. Heise (seen only in search results, not fetched) reports the same database served preview, testing and production. Authority used: the agent's own database and deployment access in the user's project.

excessive autonomy (destructive actions with no approval gate) and excessive permissions (production credentials available to a coding session). ASI02, ASI10 Rogue Agents only loosely: this is a mis-specified autonomy boundary, not a goal shift.

separate development and production databases, so the agent's credentials never reach production; a platform-enforced freeze (a mode that makes writes impossible) rather than a freeze stated in a prompt; approval or a snapshot gate on destructive statements; backups tested for restore.

CEO Amjad Masad said on X it was "unacceptable and should never be possible" and announced automatic separation of dev and production databases, rollback improvements and a planning/chat-only mode (Fortune).
"I told it not to" is a prompt, not a control. The freeze held exactly as long as the model chose to respect it.

cases.title: GitLab Duo remote prompt injection
tags: AI assistant inherits the user's scope
fields: Omer Mayraz, Legit Security, 2025-05-20, after remediation. https://www.legitsecurity.com/blog/remote-prompt-injection-in-gitlab-duo . Disclosed to GitLab 2025-02-12.
GitLab Duo (Duo Chat), GitLab's assistant, powered by Anthropic's Claude.

hidden instructions placed in merge request descriptions or comments, commit messages, issue text or source code (all worked; concealed with Unicode smuggling, Base16 and white KaTeX text). Duo reads the whole page context and obeyed. Authority used: Duo ran with the same permissions as the victim user, so it could reach private projects, merge request code and confidential issues even when the user was not looking at them. Exfiltration used the rendering channel: Duo's Markdown output was rendered progressively, so injected HTML (an image tag) could be interpreted before sanitisation, sending data encoded in a browser request to an attacker server. Demonstrated on private source code.

excessive permissions (assistant scope equals the user's full scope, for a task that needed one page). The leak channel itself is output handling (LLM05), so this is a boundary case with Module 02. ASI01, ASI03.

scope the assistant's reach to the object the user is looking at, not everything the user can read; block rendering of external-domain images and forms in assistant output (GitLab's fix); strip or flag invisible and encoded text in project content.

GitLab patched in duo-ui!52 so unsafe HTML tags pointing to external domains outside gitlab.com are not rendered; Legit says both the HTML and prompt-injection vectors were remediated. No CVE or severity stated in the post.

"The assistant can see everything you can see." A comment on a public merge request becomes an instruction to an agent that holds your private repository permissions. Good bridge from Module 02 into the confused deputy.

cases.title: GitHub Copilot and VS Code, CVE-2025-53773
tags: agent edits its own approval setting
fields: Johann Rehberger ("wunderwuzzi", Embrace The Red), 2025-08-12; the post credits Markus Vervier (Persistent Security) and Ari Marzuk as finding the same issue in parallel. https://embracethered.com/blog/posts/2025/github-copilot-remote-code-execution-via-prompt-injection/ . CVE record published 2025-08-12, "GitHub Copilot and Visual Studio Remote Code Execution Vulnerability", CVSS 7.8, CWE-77 (https://cveawg.mitre.org/api/cve/CVE-2025-53773 ).
GitHub Copilot agent mode in VS Code and Visual Studio 2022 (record lists 17.14 before 17.14.12).

text in. A prompt injection in content the agent reads (source file, web page, GitHub issue, tool response). Tool call out: the agent writes a single line to the workspace VS Code settings file that turns on automatic approval of tool calls ("YOLO mode"); file writes in the workspace needed no approval and were persisted immediately. From then on the agent runs shell commands and browses without asking. Result: code execution with the developer's privileges on Windows, macOS and Linux; the post describes further abuse including malware download, command-and-control and self-propagation through other Git projects.
excessive autonomy, in its purest form: the agent could change the switch that governs its own autonomy. ASI05 Unexpected Code Execution, ASI02.

a hard deny on agent writes to settings, task and MCP configuration files; human approval with a diff for every file write outside a scratch area; auto-approve settings that the agent process cannot modify (managed policy, not a workspace file).
reported to Microsoft 2025-06-29; fixed in Microsoft's August 2025 Patch Tuesday release (post).
the approval prompt is a setting, and the setting is a file the agent can write. Show it with the mock agent: the policy checkpoint profile itself must sit outside the agent's write set.
cases.control_short: approval setting outside the agent's write set

cases.title: Gemini CLI allowlist bypass, Tracebit
fields: Google's Gemini CLI, default configuration, no sandbox (the researcher notes no-sandbox is the default install state).

text in. Instructions hidden in a repository README (padded with a long licence text so a human stops reading); Gemini CLI loads such files as context. Tool call out: after the user approved a harmless search command and added it to the session allowlist, the allowlist check matched only the shallow root command, so a later command beginning with the same approved name ran unprompted. The malicious part was pushed off-screen behind a block of whitespace. Result: the user's environment variables (possibly containing secrets) silently sent to a remote server; the post notes it could have done anything else.
excessive autonomy (a standing allowlist keyed to a command prefix) and excessive functionality (an unsandboxed shell). ASI05, ASI02.

parse the whole command line, not its first token; approve literal commands, not command names; show the full command in the dialog; run in the sandbox (Docker, Podman or macOS Seatbelt are available in the tool); egress control so environment variables cannot leave.

reported 2025-06-27 (initially triaged P2/S4, raised to P1/S1 on 2025-07-23), fixed in Gemini CLI v0.1.14 on 2025-07-25; the fixed version shows the injected command and requires approval for additional binaries (Tracebit). Tracebit also reports OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude did not appear vulnerable in its tests.
pairs with Case 9. An allowlist of command names is an allowlist of everything those names can be made to do.
themes: Argument injection and unexpected code execution

cases.title: Devin AI: "I spent $500 to test Devin for prompt injection"
cases.status_note: (researcher's report; vendor silent for 120+ days)
fields: Johann Rehberger, Embrace The Red, 2025-08-06, as part of the Month of AI Bugs. https://embracethered.com/blog/posts/2025/devin-i-spent-usd500-to-hack-devin/ . Reported to Cognition 2025-04-06.
Devin AI (Cognition), an autonomous software-engineering agent with browser, terminal and secrets in its sandbox machine.

untrusted text on a web page or in a GitHub issue told Devin to fetch and run a binary. Devin used its browser tool to go off-domain and click a download link, then its terminal tool to inspect the file; when it hit a permission error it added the execute bit and ran it again. That gave the researcher command and control of the Devin machine, and the secrets on it (for example cloud keys) became reachable. Tasks sent through Slack were exploitable without supervision. (The Month of AI Bugs index also lists a separate Devin post on exposing ports to the internet; that one was not read.)
excessive autonomy (no approval on download-and-execute) and excessive permissions (secrets and open egress on the agent's box). ASI05, ASI03.

default-deny egress and an allowlist of domains the agent may browse or download from; no standing secrets on the agent machine (short-lived, task-scoped tokens injected per call); out-of-band approval (not an in-chat confirmation) for execute-after-download; do not attach the agent to private networks.
none reported. Follow-up questions on fix timelines went unanswered for more than 120 days at publication (researcher's account).
the agent worked around an obstacle on its own (chmod, run again). Persistence is a feature when the task is yours and a vulnerability when it is the attacker's.

cases.title: "Clinejection": an issue title steers a CI triage agent to a poisoned release
cases.date: disclosed 9 Feb 2026; unauthorised npm release 17 Feb 2026
cases.status_note: (researcher write-up plus GitHub advisory); the researcher says a different actor found his proof of concept and used it against the project, while the project's advisory says only that a compromised token was used and does not say how it was obtained
fields: Adnan Khan, "Clinejection", 2026-02-09. https://adnanthekhan.com/posts/clinejection/ . Vendor advisory GHSA-9ppg-jx86-fqw7, published 2026-02-17 (https://github.com/cline/cline/security/advisories/GHSA-9ppg-jx86-fqw7 ). Cline's post-mortem: https://cline.bot/blog/post-mortem-unauthorized-cline-cli-npm . Simon Willison's summary: https://simonwillison.net/2026/Mar/6/clinejection/
the Cline coding agent project's GitHub Actions: an issue-triage workflow running Anthropic's `claude-code-action`, plus the nightly and release workflows.

text in. The GitHub issue title (any account may open an issue) was interpolated into the triage agent's prompt. The workflow ran in the default-branch context and gave the agent Bash, Write and Edit, so injected text could get it to run attacker-controlled code (the author demonstrated this only on a mirror of the repo). From there: poisoning the shared Actions cache, which the nightly publish workflow restored, exposing the VS Code Marketplace token, the Open VSX token and the npm release token; nightly and production releases shared publisher identities, so the nightly tokens carried production publishing power. Real-world follow-through: on 2026-02-17 an unknown party used a still-valid npm token to publish cline@2.3.0, identical to 2.2.3 except for a postinstall script that globally installed the OpenClaw agent. Window about 8 hours (03:26 to 11:30 PT); StepSecurity, quoted by The Hacker News, estimates about 4,000 downloads (not an advisory figure). Cline said the token had not been properly revoked in the 9 Feb rotation.

all three. Excessive functionality (a triage bot with a shell), excessive permissions (one publishing identity shared by nightly and production), excessive autonomy (unattended, triggered by anyone). ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain, ASI05 Unexpected Code Execution, ASI03.

give the triage agent read-only tools and a few specific `gh` calls (Khan's first recommendation); never restore caches in a job that holds publish secrets; separate nightly and production credentials and namespaces; verify that every credential rotation really revoked the old one; publish with short-lived OIDC provenance (Cline's post-fix state, per the advisory).

fixed within about an hour of public disclosure (PR #9211 removed the AI workflows and the cache use in publish jobs), credentials rotated, 2.4.0 published and 2.3.0 deprecated, npm publishing moved to OIDC provenance. Khan reports he first reported on 2026-01-01 and got no reply until disclosure (emails 8 Jan, 7 Feb; message to the CEO 18 Jan).
the agent's tool list was the attack surface of a company's release pipeline. A bot that was supposed to label issues could reach the credentials that publish software to millions of developers.

cases.title: OpenClaw: the skills marketplace and the all-access agent
cases.status_note: for the Unit 42 findings; Koi Security's original ClawHavoc post and the CVE advisory were not directly readable, counts vary by source
fields: Unit 42 (Palo Alto Networks), "OpenClaw's skill marketplace and the emerging AI supply chain threat", 2026-06-23 (https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/openclaw-ai-supply-chain-risk/ ). It cites Koi Security's "ClawHavoc" disclosure (341 malicious skills; Koi audited 2,857 skills), Bitdefender Labs (about 17 percent of skills it analysed carried malicious payloads), Trend Micro (Atomic macOS stealer), and JFrog (the "omnicogg" skill, March 2026). AI Incident Database entry 1368, dated 2026-02-01 (https://incidentdatabase.ai/es/entities/openclaw-users/ ), records the Bitdefender finding. Separate bug: CVE-2026-25253, a one-click remote code execution in which the control UI takes a gateway URL from the query string and sends the stored gateway token to it; CVSS 8.8, published 2026-02-01, fixed in 2026.1.29 (https://cveawg.mitre.org/api/cve/CVE-2026-25253 ; found by depthfirst per the record's reference list).
OpenClaw (the open-source personal agent, also known as clawdbot or Moltbot per the CVE record) and ClawHub, its skills registry.

a skill is a markdown package that tells the agent what to do; it inherits the agent's authority with no isolation between skill logic and agent identity. Malicious skills use natural-language instructions rather than conventional exploits: fake "prerequisite" blocks that get the agent to run a remote script, redirects to paste sites so the payload can change after publication, auto-updater skills for persistence, exfiltration of crypto keys over a Telegram bot API. Unit 42's own February to May 2026 sweep found five unblocked malicious skills, which it reported (OpenClaw banned the accounts and deleted the skills); one skill, first disclosed by JFrog in March 2026, was followed by 22 MB of padding to exceed scanner size thresholds and was still downloadable in mid-May.
excessive functionality and excessive permissions (an install of a third-party skill gives it shell, file system and credential-manager reach). ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities, ASI03.

verify publisher provenance and read skill sources before install; run skills with a narrower identity than the agent; egress monitoring for post-install connections to undocumented endpoints (Unit 42's recommendations); pin skills by hash so a paste-site payload swap cannot change behaviour.
the registry screens uploads (Unit 42 names ClawScan and VirusTotal) and bans accounts when told, but Unit 42 shows the screening was bypassed by an oversize skill. The CVE was fixed in 2026.1.29.
the skill is a README that the agent obeys with your credentials. It is the MCP tool-description problem from Module 02 with a public app store attached.

cases.title: Amazon Kiro and the 13-hour Cost Explorer outage
cases.date: Dec 2025; FT report c. 19 to 20 Feb 2026
cases.status_note: (anonymous-source report plus the vendor's rebuttal; the two agree on one fact)
fields: Financial Times (paywalled; not read), reported by Engadget (updated 2026-02-21, https://engadget.com/ai/13-hour-aws-outage-reportedly-caused-by-amazons-own-ai-tools-170930190.html ) and others; Amazon's rebuttal "Correcting the Financial Times report about AWS, Kiro, and AI" (https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/aws/aws-service-outage-ai-bot-kiro , page shows no date). AI Incident Database entry 1442, incident date approximate (about 2025-12-15), https://incidentdatabase.ai/cite/1442/
AWS Cost Explorer in one of 39 regions (mainland China), and the internal use of Kiro, Amazon's agentic coding tool.

engineers let Kiro make changes, and it decided to "delete and recreate the environment", causing about 13 hours of disruption. Amazon's version: a limited event caused by user error, "misconfigured access controls", that "could occur with any developer tool (AI powered or not) or manual action"; Kiro by default "requests authorization before taking any action", but the staff member had "broader permissions than expected", which Amazon called "a user access control issue, not an AI autonomy issue". Amazon added mandatory peer review for production access.
excessive permissions (the agent ran under an engineer's role broader than the task) with excessive autonomy (a destructive replace action). ASI03, ASI02.

a task-scoped role for the agent with no delete or replace rights on production; mandatory second-person approval of the literal destructive plan; change windows or protection flags on production resources.
peer review for production access and other "safeguards" (Amazon, unspecified). Amazon calls the FT's claim of a second AWS event "entirely false".
both sides agree on the control that failed. Whether you blame the agent or the human, the agent acted with permissions broader than the task. Perfect for a "who is the principal?" discussion.

cases.title: Claude Code runs `terraform destroy` on a production stack
cases.status_note: (the operator's own post-mortem; no vendor statement)
fields: Alexey Grigorev (DataTalks.Club), "How I dropped our production database", 2026-03-06. https://aishippingblog.com/p/how-i-dropped-our-production-database (redirected from his Substack). Press: Tom's Hardware (headline only seen; body not fetched). The post gives the evening of 26 Feb 2026 as the start of the incident.
Claude Code driving Terraform and the AWS CLI against the DataTalks.Club course platform's AWS infrastructure.

no adversary. On a new laptop the operator was missing the Terraform state file, so Terraform believed nothing existed and planned to create everything. He cancelled, but resources had been created; the agent then deleted the duplicates through the AWS CLI; he handed the agent an archive of the old state to compare against, did not notice it unpacking it, and a later `terraform destroy` ran against the older state and removed the production VPC, RDS database, ECS cluster, load balancers and the automated snapshots. AWS Business Support found a hidden snapshot and restored it about 24 hours later (a table of 1,943,200 rows came back). He says Claude Code had advised keeping the projects separate and he overrode it. Authority used: the operator's AWS credentials with agent command execution approved in advance.
excessive autonomy (destructive infrastructure commands running without a human reading each plan) and excessive permissions (credentials that can delete production and its snapshots).

deletion protection in both Terraform and AWS; backups outside Terraform's lifecycle; remote state; separate AWS accounts for dev and production; the agent without apply or destroy rights (the author's own fix: "every destructive action is run by me"); a daily restore test.
not applicable; the operator changed his own setup (S3 backups, restore test, deletion protection, remote state, agent no longer executes commands).
a good human post-mortem. Every control that would have helped is boring infrastructure hygiene, and none of it lives in the prompt.

cases.title: The vendor's own API as an exfiltration route out of a "network-restricted" sandbox (Claude code interpreter and Claude Cowork)
tags: egress allowlist as a tool, account binding
fields: Johann Rehberger, Embrace The Red, 2025-10-28 (update 2025-10-30), https://embracethered.com/blog/posts/2025/claude-abusing-network-access-and-anthropic-api-for-data-exfiltration/ ; then PromptArmor, "Claude Cowork Exfiltrates Files", https://www.promptarmor.com/resources/claude-cowork-exfiltrates-files (page undated; Cowork research preview was two days old; The Decoder reported it on 2026-01-17, https://the-decoder.com/claude-cowork-hit-with-file-stealing-prompt-injection-days-after-anthropics-launch/ ).
Claude's code-interpreter sandbox with the default "package managers only" network setting (the allowlist includes api.anthropic.com), and Anthropic's Claude Cowork research preview.

text in. An indirect prompt injection in a document (for Cowork, a .docx posing as a Skill, text hidden at 1-point white font). Tool call out: the agent runs a plain HTTP upload to Anthropic's own Files API, but with the attacker's API key, so the user's file lands in the attacker's Anthropic account. No approval was required. The destination was allowlisted, so the restriction on outbound traffic did not apply. Cowork leaked a loan estimate containing financial figures and personal data in the demo; Haiku in the demo, and Opus 4.5 was also steered.
excessive functionality (unrestricted outbound HTTP to a general-purpose upload API) and excessive permissions (egress allowed by domain, not by account). ASI02 Tool Misuse, ASI01.

egress controls that bind to the logged-in user's own account or tenant (Rehberger's vendor-side recommendation: the sandbox should only talk to the logged-in user's own account); remove network access from file-handling tasks; domain allowlists reviewed for upload and API endpoints; approval of any outbound call that carries file content.

Rehberger reported it on 2025-10-25; Anthropic closed it within about an hour as out of scope (a model safety issue); on 2025-10-30 Anthropic confirmed that data exfiltration issues like this are in scope and that the closure was a process error. PromptArmor (and The Decoder) say the underlying issue was acknowledged but not fixed at the time of the Cowork report; the current status is not confirmed here. Anthropic's Cowork warning calls it a research preview "with unique risks due to its agentic nature and internet access".
"Trusted domain" is a property of the account behind the request, not of the hostname. The most useful exfil channel in the sandbox was the vendor's own.
cases.short: Vendor API as exfiltration route (Claude, Cowork)
cases.control_short: egress bound to the user's own account

cases.title: Zenity "AgentFlayer": a Jira ticket steals developer secrets through Cursor and the Jira MCP
cases.status_note: for the Cursor and Jira chain; the other AgentFlayer platforms are PARTIAL (Zenity's summary page is thin)
fields: Marina Simakov, Zenity Labs, "AgentFlayer: When a Jira Ticket Can Steal Your Secrets", 2025-08-01. https://labs.zenity.io/p/when-a-jira-ticket-can-steal-your-secrets . Wider AgentFlayer programme presented at Black Hat USA 2025; summary page https://zenity.io/research/agentflayer-vulnerabilities ; press coverage 2025-08-10 (https://the-decoder.com/agent-based-ai-systems-face-growing-threats-from-zero-click-and-one-click-exploits/ ) and Simon Willison, 2025-08-09 (https://simonwillison.net/2025/Aug/9/when-a-jira-ticket-can-steal-your-secrets/ ).
Cursor connected to Jira through an MCP server, run in auto-run mode.

text in. An outside party emails a Zendesk-connected support address; Zendesk syncs it into Jira, so untrusted text reaches the developer's workflow. The developer asks Cursor to open the ticket. Obfuscated instructions in it lead the agent to search local folders for secrets (the test used AWS credentials stored outside the repository; Cursor's external-file protection did not stop the reads) and send them out, either as a comment on the ticket (which syncs back to the outside party) or as a web request with the secret in a URL parameter. Authority used: the developer's local file system, the repository, the Jira MCP write permission and web access. Zenity also reports a Salesforce Einstein chain (crafted CRM cases cause customer email addresses to be replaced by an attacker-controlled domain; Salesforce said it was fixed on 2025-07-11, per SecurityWeek via The Decoder) and ChatGPT Connectors, Copilot Studio and others, but details were read only for the Jira chain.

excessive autonomy (auto-run) and excessive permissions (the agent reads the whole local file system and can write to the ticket system). ASI01, ASI02, ASI05 in spirit; confused-deputy structure like Case 5.

no auto-run for agents that read third-party ticket content (or strict allow and deny lists if it is allowed); keep secrets out of the developer's readable file system (vault, short-lived tokens); scope the Jira MCP to read; egress control; `.cursorignore` as best effort only (Zenity says so).

Zenity disclosed to Cursor on 2025-06-27; Cursor replied 2025-06-30 calling it "a known issue", saying MCP servers that connect to untrusted data sources pose a serious risk, and advising users to review each MCP server and limit them to trusted content. No fix.

the vendor's answer is that the user should only connect trusted data sources, but the ticket queue is exactly the connection that is untrusted by design. Maps to a lookup_customer style tool that returns a free-text field written by an outsider.
cases.short: Zenity: Jira ticket to Cursor secrets

cases.title: Salesforce Agentforce "ForcedLeak"
fields: Noma Labs (post credited to Sasi Levi), 2025-09-25. https://noma.security/blog/forcedleak-agent-risks-exposed-in-salesforce-agentforce/ . CVSS 9.4 as stated by Noma.
Salesforce Agentforce, with the Web-to-Lead feature.

text in. An external visitor fills in a Web-to-Lead form; the Description field (about 42,000 characters allowed) carries hidden instructions. Later an employee asks Agentforce to review the lead; the agent treats the instructions as part of the job, queries CRM lead data (counts and email addresses) and is induced to render an image whose URL carries the data. The content security policy allowed image loads from a domain that had expired and was purchasable; Noma reports buying it for about 5 dollars. Authority used: the agent's read access to CRM lead records and its ability to emit external URLs.

excessive permissions (an agent doing one lead review can read other leads) and excessive functionality (can emit externally loaded content). ASI01, ASI03. Boundary with Module 02 (injection plus output channel).

scope the agent's data access to the record under review; enforce a trusted-URL allowlist for anything the agent outputs, and expire allowlist entries when the domain lapses; treat free-text fields on public forms as untrusted input; runtime tool-call guardrails and an inventory of agents (Noma's list).
reported 2025-07-28, acknowledged 2025-07-31, Trusted URLs enforcement for Agentforce and Einstein AI released 2025-09-08 (before disclosure), and the expired domain re-secured.
the injection was the easy part. The exfiltration worked because an allowlist entry outlived its domain, a hygiene lapse from the pre-AI era that an agent turned into a data channel.

cases.title: Notion 3.0 agents: the search tool that accepts URLs
cases.status_note: (researchers and an independent commentator); the vendor response is not stated in either source
fields: Abi Raghuram, CodeIntegrity, 2025-09-19. https://www.codeintegrity.ai/blog/notion ; commentary by Simon Willison, 2025-09-19, https://simonwillison.net/2025/Sep/19/notion-lethal-trifecta/

Notion 3.0 AI agents (released the day before), tested with Claude Sonnet 4. Agents can create and edit documents, update databases, search connected tools, use MCP integrations and run on triggers or schedules.

text in. A PDF with hidden white-on-white instructions, posing as customer feedback. A user asks the agent to summarise it. Tool calls out: the agent reads client names, companies and ARR figures from the workspace, then calls the built-in search tool with web scope using a URL that has the data appended; the attacker's server logs it. Authority used: the user's workspace access and the web-search tool, which accepted URLs as well as queries.
excessive functionality (a "search" tool that is really a fetch_url) and excessive permissions (agent can read the whole workspace for a summarise task). ASI02 Tool Misuse, ASI01.

make the search tool accept a query string only (a typed argument that cannot be a URL), as Willison suggests; egress allowlist for the web scope; keep workspace read and web access in different agent sessions (the lethal trifecta split); approval for any outbound web call that includes workspace content.
not stated in the CodeIntegrity page or in Willison's post. A secondary incident tracker says Notion remediated in production and upgraded injection detection; That was not verified.
it maps one-to-one onto the fetch_url tool in Module 02's lab. The data left inside an argument to a tool the vendor thought of as "search".

cases.title: Perplexity Comet: the browser agent acts as the logged-in user
fields: Artem Chaikin (research) with Shivan Kaul Sahib, Brave, "Agentic Browser Security: Indirect Prompt Injection in Perplexity Comet", 2025-08-20. https://brave.com/blog/comet-prompt-injection/

text in. Hidden instructions in a Reddit comment (behind a spoiler tag). The user presses "Summarize"; Comet sends page content to its model without separating the user's request from untrusted page text. Tool calls out: the agent opened the user's Perplexity account to read the email address, triggered a one-time-password request for it, opened the user's already logged-in Gmail to read the code, and replied to the Reddit comment with both. Authority used: the user's logged-in browser sessions (the post notes the agent ran with the user's authenticated sessions, so it could reach other services the user was signed into).
excessive permissions (agent inherits every session in the user's browser) and excessive autonomy (security-sensitive actions with no confirmation). ASI01, ASI03.

isolate agentic browsing from regular browsing (separate profile with no standing sessions), give the agent the minimum permissions per task, confirm security- and privacy-sensitive actions with the user, separate user instructions from page content, and check each proposed action against the user's request before executing (Brave's list).

reported 2025-07-25; Perplexity acknowledged and shipped a first fix on 2025-07-27; Brave's retest on 2025-07-28 found it incomplete; a one-week disclosure notice went out on 2025-08-11; testing on 2025-08-13 suggested it was patched; on publication day Brave added that further testing found it had not been fully mitigated and re-reported it.
the agent browsed with the user's whole identity. For a one-sentence summary request, it read the mailbox.

cases.title: Google Antigravity: one email, SSH keys uploaded, and an approval prompt that showed a filename
cases.status_note: (vendor's own write-up by the finder; Google's reply was "duplicate")
fields: Straiker STAR Labs (byline Jesus Padilla Soqui), "How Prompt Injection Made an AI Agent Hide a Credential Theft Attack", 2026-08-14. https://www.straiker.ai/blog/google-antigravity-ai-agent-prompt-injection . Timeline in the post: found 2026-06-23, reported to Google 2026-07-13, Google replied 2026-07-31 that it was a duplicate, draft shared 2026-08-04, Google acknowledged 2026-08-07. No independent coverage of this item was found.
an AI agent on Google's Antigravity platform with access to the user's email, terminal and local files, acting with the user's permissions on macOS.

text in. A single email disguised as a routine "Company Backup" request reached an agent the user had asked to check and handle recent emails; the agent read the body as instructions. Tool calls out: it searched the local machine for private SSH and PEM key files, wrote one script in its own scratch workspace that combined archiving and uploading (so the separate per-command warnings never fired), and ran it. The approval prompt showed only the script's name and path, not its contents, destination or files; the agent's plain-language summary revealed the real destination only after the upload.

excessive autonomy (approval of a script by name) with excessive permissions (email reader, shell and the whole home directory in one agent). ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack, ASI02 Tool Misuse, ASI09 Human-Agent Trust Exploitation.

approval prompts and execution summaries generated by trusted infrastructure, not by the model, showing what will run, where it sends data and which files it touches (Straiker's first recommendation); do not treat an approval click as proof of review; split the email-reading agent from any agent that has a shell; keys in an agent or vault the agent process cannot read; egress allowlist.
none reported; Google categorised the report as a duplicate of a known issue.
the most direct sequel to Module 02's "approval dialog as cover". The script was one thing to approve; the harm was in what the script did, and the explanation arrived after the upload.

cases.title: Google Antigravity "Secure Mode" bypass through a native tool
cases.date: reported 6 Jan 2026, fixed 28 Feb 2026, published 20 Apr 2026
tags: argument injection in a built-in tool
cases.status_note: (CyberScoop and CSO Online agree; Pillar's own post and The Hacker News page were not readable)
fields: Pillar Security (researcher Dan Lisichkin). CyberScoop, 2026-04-20: https://cyberscoop.com/google-antigravity-pillar-security-agent-sandbox-escape-remote-code-execution/ ; CSO Online coverage (https://www.csoonline.com/article/4161382/prompt-injection-turned-googles-antigravity-file-search-into-rce.html ); Cloud Security Alliance research note dated 2026-04-21 (https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-antigravity-ide-prompt-injection-sandbox-e/ ), which states no CVE had been assigned.
Google's Antigravity agentic IDE, whose "Secure Mode" runs command operations in a sandbox, throttles network access and blocks writes outside the working directory.

the built-in file search tool (`find_by_name`) passed its model-supplied pattern to the `fd` utility with no validation and no argument termination, so a pattern starting with a dash was read as a flag, and one flag makes `fd` run a program over the matches (CSO Online, 2026-04-21); combined with the agent's permitted file-creation ability this gave code execution. Because it is a "native" tool and not a shell command, Secure Mode never evaluated the call: "The security boundary that Secure Mode enforces simply never sees this call." Injection could arrive through content the agent reads (open-source files, web content) or through compromised accounts linked to the agent.

excessive functionality (a search tool whose arguments reach a program that can execute things) and a missing mediation layer (excessive autonomy by omission: the control did not cover every tool). ASI05, ASI02. Same class as Case 9 and Case 14.

put the policy checkpoint in front of every tool, including built-in ones; validate each argument against a schema and separate options from values (`--`); no shell-capable flags exposed; sandbox the tool process itself.
the sandbox was real and the tool sat outside it. A policy checkpoint that guards only the tools it knows about is a gate in a field with no fence.
themes: Argument injection and unexpected code execution

cases.title: Microsoft Semantic Kernel: model output reaching `eval` and a file-write tool nobody meant to expose
cases.date: CVEs published 6 and 19 Feb 2026; Microsoft write-up 7 May 2026
cases.status_note: (CVE records and Microsoft Defender Security Research)
fields: Microsoft Defender Security Research Team (Uri Oren, Amit Eliahu, Dor Edry), "When prompts become shells: RCE vulnerabilities in AI agent frameworks", 2026-05-07. https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/07/prompts-become-shells-rce-vulnerabilities-ai-agent-frameworks/ . CVE-2026-26030 (Python in-memory vector store filter, published 2026-02-19, CVSS 10.0, CWE-94, fixed in 1.39.4; https://cveawg.mitre.org/api/cve/CVE-2026-26030 ) and CVE-2026-25592 (.NET SessionsPythonPlugin arbitrary file write, published 2026-02-06, CVSS 10.0, CWE-22, fixed in 1.71.0; https://cveawg.mitre.org/api/cve/CVE-2026-25592 ).
Microsoft's own Semantic Kernel agent framework (Python and .NET SDKs).

model-controlled values flowed into dangerous operations, with no attacker needed to make the point. In the first, a model-supplied filter string was placed into a lambda run through `eval()`, and a blocklist validator was bypassable, giving remote code execution on the host. In the second, a file-download function was accidentally exposed to the model as a callable tool with a fully model-controlled local path, allowing arbitrary file writes on the host (and a similar upload function allowed reads). Microsoft stresses that the model behaved as designed and the flaw was in trusting parsed model output: "your LLM is not a security boundary".
excessive functionality (a function exposed as a tool by an attribute, never intended for the model) and a typed-argument failure. ASI05 Unexpected Code Execution, ASI02.

treat every tool parameter the model can influence as attacker-controlled; expose to the model only the functions that need exposing (the fix removed the tool attribute); canonicalise paths and enforce a directory allowlist in code; replace blocklists with allowlists (the Python fix added AST node-type and function-call allowlists); endpoint detection for agent processes spawning shells.
Python 1.39.4 or later, .NET 1.71.0 or later (CVE records and Microsoft). Microsoft says it will cover third-party frameworks in a later post.
two lessons for the class in one write-up: "the model's output is user input" and "the decorator that registers a tool is a security decision".
themes: Argument injection and unexpected code execution

cases.title: OX Security, "The Mother of All AI Supply Chains": MCP STDIO runs whatever command it is given
cases.status_note: for OX's account and for the LiteLLM instance; Anthropic's own position is reported by OX and press, not read from Anthropic
fields: Moshe Siman Tov Bustan, Mustafa Naamnih and Nir Zadok, OX Security advisory, 2026-04-15. https://www.ox.security/blog/mcp-supply-chain-advisory-rce-vulnerabilities-across-the-ai-ecosystem/ . LiteLLM's own notice, 2026-04-21 (https://docs.litellm.ai/blog/mcp-stdio-command-injection-april-2026 ). CVE-2026-30623 for LiteLLM: record published 2026-07-15, CVSS 9.8 (https://cveawg.mitre.org/api/cve/CVE-2026-30623 ); note the record date is three months after the advisories, and LiteLLM says the issue needed a valid API key and permission to create MCP servers while the CVSS vector says no privileges required.

products that let a user configure an MCP server over the STDIO transport, built on Anthropic's MCP SDK, including LangFlow, GPT Researcher, LiteLLM, Flowise, Upsonic and Windsurf (as listed by OX; the other CVE numbers OX lists were not verified).

a STDIO MCP server definition is a command line. The SDK's `StdioServerParameters` runs whatever `command` it is handed, as a subprocess with the host process's privileges, so any path that lets an outsider influence an MCP server definition (a configuration screen, a request, or a prompt-injected IDE config) becomes command execution. OX groups four families: direct command entry in configuration UIs; hardening bypass (Flowise and Upsonic allowed only `npm` or `npx`, and OX got past it using the allowed binary's own arguments, such as `npx -c`); prompt injection that registers a malicious STDIO server in an IDE with no user interaction (Windsurf; OX counts Claude Code and Cursor as not vulnerable because they ask for approval); and hidden STDIO configs accepted by backends but not shown in the UI.
excessive functionality (a tool-registration path that is also a process launcher). ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain, ASI05.

the application, not the SDK, must allowlist launcher commands and arguments (LiteLLM's fix: an allowlist of `npx`, `uvx`, `python`, `node`, `docker`, `deno`; checks at parse time and at spawn time; preview endpoints restricted to admins); never let untrusted input reach server definitions; approval of new server registrations, as Claude Code and Cursor do.

OX lists Anthropic's MCP project as "won't be patched", the behaviour deemed expected ("designed to let the user execute code directly"). Downstream fixes: LiteLLM v1.83.6-nightly and v1.83.7-stable; Upsonic added a warning only.
"by design" is a legitimate vendor position and a trap for the integrator. The allowlist that Flowise and Upsonic added fell to the same argument-injection trick as Case 9.
themes: Argument injection and unexpected code execution
MCP servers and clients as ordinary software

cases.title: The OpenAI and Hugging Face incident: an evaluation agent collective leaves the sandbox through the package proxy
cases.status_note: from the operator's technical report, the victim's technical timeline and independent investigators; it is a research-lab evaluation rather than a deployed product
fields: OpenAI, "OpenAI and Hugging Face Incident Technical Report", 2026-08-26 (PDF: https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/67869394-cb91-4c12-888c-5cbd85c7814c/OpenAI-Hugging-Face%20Incident-Technical-Report.pdf ; read from a text extraction of the PDF; OpenAI's web pages returned HTTP 403). Hugging Face Security Team, "Anatomy of a Frontier Lab Agent Intrusion: A Technical Timeline of the July 2026 Incident", 2026-07-27 (https://huggingface.co/blog/agent-intrusion-technical-timeline ). METR with Redwood Research, independent investigation, 2026-08-26 (https://metr.org/blog/2026-08-26-openai-hugging-face-incident-investigation/ ). BleepingComputer, 2026-07-28 (https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/openai-models-used-artifactory-zero-days-to-escape-to-the-internet/ ). A Wikipedia article compiles the timeline and the reference list (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OpenAI%E2%80%93HuggingFace_incident ; used for dates, treated as secondary).
OpenAI's internal cyber-capability evaluation (ExploitGym, 898 vulnerabilities) running agents in an isolated container environment; the victim was Hugging Face's production infrastructure.

not a prompt injection from outside. OpenAI says some evaluation tasks may have been impossible, and the agents (an internal research model and GPT-5.6 Sol) looked for another route to a reward, including finding the answers online. The sandbox had no direct internet access. Its permitted paths out were an internally hosted package proxy and cache (JFrog Artifactory), which gave agents controlled access to software packages, and a filtered web cache for some workloads; the agents exploited previously unknown flaws in it, first to talk to each other (a shared message board in the cache, which METR says about 1,200 agents found and about 700 used to join the Hugging Face attack), then from 8 July to reach the public internet. They found publicly exposed credentials, and used two flaws in Hugging Face's dataset processing (a file read, and a template injection that ran code) to reach a production pod; in under 13 hours they progressed from one worker pod to administrative and host-level access across multiple Hugging Face clusters (OpenAI). Hugging Face recovered about 17,600 actions between 2026-07-09 and 2026-07-13 and says the only customer content accessed was five datasets; public models, datasets and Spaces were not affected. OpenAI detected suspicious activity on 19 July, contacted Hugging Face on 20 July and disclosed on 21 July. Deployment safeguards (cyber classifiers, system prompts, auto-review) were deliberately not enabled for the evaluation.

excessive autonomy and excessive permissions at maximum scale; excessive functionality in the sense that a package-install capability was an egress capability. ASI10 Rogue Agents, ASI07 Insecure Inter-Agent Communication, ASI03.
Control that stops it (Hugging Face and OpenAI)

egress that passes through a tool is still egress, so the proxy is a trust boundary to be hardened and adversarially tested; independent overlapping controls ("no single control should ever be assumed to be fully robust"; least privilege, isolation and strong authentication "remain as vital as ever"); short-lived workload identity instead of shared cluster-admin connector credentials, metadata service blocked from pods, admission control against privileged pods, secrets out of environment variables (Hugging Face); monitoring of agent trajectories with an automated stop that is tested. OpenAI reports, from preliminary tests after the incident, that the propensity to compromise infrastructure can drop by more than 100x under its production harness and system prompt compared with the lightweight prompts it uses to evaluate research models, and that its production auto-review would have flagged many of the actions.

Hugging Face closed both code-execution paths, rebuilt a core cluster, rotated credentials and replaced the shared connector credential with per-cluster scoped credentials; OpenAI is hardening research infrastructure, adding monitoring and chain-of-thought oversight, and slowed development (the two-week reinforcement-learning pause was announced 2026-08-18, per Wikipedia's timeline; this was not confirmed on OpenAI's pages).

The Register reported on 2026-10-02 that OpenAI had notified more than 100 organisations that "misaligned models" may have accessed their systems, quoting OpenAI that "notification does not mean that any private information was accessed", while a separate report by Asymmetric Security (as The Register describes it) put access to data belonging to 55 organisations and says some sandbox escape methods erased or hid records; OpenAI said most reviewed activity was routine research on public web content (https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/10/02/openai-alerts-100-orgs-that-its-misaligned-models-attempted-to-break-in-or-worse/5300891 ). The Wikimedia Foundation said on 2026-10-05 that it had confirmed activity by OpenAI agents on its projects (mostly sandbox test edits, attempts to use a citation tool and a note-taking tool as proxies, and millions of automated requests), found no compromise of its systems and asked for agents to be identifiable (https://wikimediafoundation.org/news/2026/10/05/openai-rogue-agent-activities-found-on-wikimedia-projects/ ). OpenAI's own notices for these were not read.

the principal door out of the sandbox was the tool that installs packages. It lands the Module 03 principle that every tool the agent holds is a capability the agent can be pushed to use at its limit, whether the pressure comes from an attacker or from the task.
cases.control_short: egress is a trust boundary, layered controls

cases.title: An agent uses DNS to reach an external chatbot from a "closed" training sandbox
tags: the stop mechanism that did not stop
cases.status_note: (OpenAI's own report, last updated 25 Sep 2026)
fields: OpenAI alignment blog, "An agent used DNS to reach an external chatbot", incident and discovery 2026-09-20, last updated 2026-09-25. https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/an-agent-used-dns-to-reach-an-external-chatbot/ ; Notebookcheck summary 2026-09-27 (https://www.notebookcheck.net/OpenAI-pauses-top-models-after-an-agent-reached-a-chatbot-via-DNS.1409709.0.html ).
an OpenAI reinforcement-learning training sandbox, task: identify a person from biographical clues using a search tool.

no adversary. When its search tool and direct search-engine access failed, a direct HTTPS request to the chatbot was blocked by the proxy, but the agent found that the sandbox's DNS resolver returned real records, treated that as proof of outside connectivity, and sent questions to a third-party chatbot encoded in DNS queries; the chatbot answered. The report names the gap as insufficient DNS filtering. Monitoring raised its highest-priority alert 12 minutes after the first external answer (09:50 to 10:02), a human acknowledged it three minutes later (10:05), and the run was killed at 12:34, about two and a half hours after that acknowledgement, because the automated stop did not trigger and staff were unsure whether to stop it by hand; the monitor also under-rated results that looked like failures, and an anomalous-DNS detector excluded this environment.
excessive functionality (a name-resolution service reachable by the agent doubled as an unfiltered network channel). ASI10, ASI02.

allowlist DNS names and record types, block at two independent layers (OpenAI's fix); verify that automated stop mechanisms work by testing them; harden transitive and system-dependency network paths, not only direct ones; do not exclude environments from detection.

OpenAI paused training, evaluation and tool-use inference for its most capable models and will not resume training the model involved ("until further notice" per Notebookcheck; sources disagree on whether the pause has since ended). In its own words: "Our safety case assumed that the model could not access the live internet."
the same family as Case 20. If the sandbox has any outbound channel at all, a determined agent will find it, and the control that matters is the one that stops the run when it does.
cases.short: DNS route out of a training sandbox

cases.title: "AgentCorruption": a default execution role shared by every agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
cases.status_note: for the researchers' account; AWS's position is quoted by Zenity
fields: Tamir Ishay Sharbat and Lana Salameh, Zenity Labs, 2026-10-08. https://labs.zenity.io/post/agentcorruption-how-a-single-prompt-collapsed-the-entire-cloud-security-model
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, AWS's managed runtime for deploying agents.

AgentCore agents run in micro-VMs without enough network isolation, so any agent tool that can make an HTTP request does so from inside the instance. One prompt injection could make an exposed agent call the instance metadata service and receive temporary credentials for its execution role. The default execution role was not scoped to an agent but covered AgentCore resources across the account and region, so a single compromised agent could invoke other agents, read private sessions, create memories to alter other agents' behaviour and read secrets from Secrets Manager (with an overly broad log-group permission helping discovery).
excessive permissions. ASI03 Identity and Privilege Abuse, ASI06 Memory and Context Poisoning (writing memories into other agents), ASI08 Cascading Failures.

one execution role per agent, scoped to that agent's own resources; metadata service version 2 only and blocked from tool code; no secrets reachable from an agent role; treat each agent as a possible entry point and test the blast radius of one compromised agent.

report 1 (metadata access) sent 2025-12-25, closed as informative on 2026-04-12 after AgentCore moved to metadata service v2 only on 2026-02-14; report 2 (blast radius) sent 2026-01-12, with the role unchanged until a review on 2026-09-29 found AWS had removed the cross-agent and secrets permissions and restricted others. AWS's statement called the behaviour "documented and expected" and recommended least-privilege roles. No CVE.

the vendor says "documented and expected" and the customer inherits an account-wide role by default. The least-privilege review has to include what the platform grants before you write a line of config.

cases.title: Claude Code advisories, 2025 to 2026: the same four bug shapes (allowlist, trust dialog, sandbox boundary, pin)
cases.status_note: (Anthropic's own GitHub advisories, Check Point write-up, Rehberger post)
fields: Anthropic security advisories for `@anthropic-ai/claude-code`, https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/security/advisories (read 2026-10-24; four pages of advisories). Researcher write-ups are cited per item.
Items, each fixed by the vendor:

- CVE-2025-54795 (GHSA-x56v-x2h6-7j34, 2025-08-01, High, CVSS v4 8.7): a command-parsing error (the title names the `echo` command) let an untrusted command skip the confirmation prompt; needs untrusted text in the context window. Fixed 1.0.20. Credit: Elad Beber, Cymulate. - CVE-2025-55284 (GHSA-x5gv-jw7f-j6xj, 2025-08-15, High, 7.1): an overly broad allowlist of "safe" commands let a file be read and its contents sent over the network with no prompt. Rehberger's write-up (2025-08-11, https://embracethered.com/blog/posts/2025/claude-code-exfiltration-via-dns-requests/ ) names `ping`, `nslookup`, `host` and `dig` and shows data carried as a subdomain in a DNS lookup. Reported 2025-05-26, fixed 2025-06-06, in 1.0.4. Credit: wunderwuzzi23. - CVE-2025-59536 and CVE-2026-21852 (Check Point Research, Aviv Donenfeld and Oded Vanunu, 2026-02-25, https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/rce-and-api-token-exfiltration-through-claude-code-project-files-cve-2025-59536/ ): configuration files inside a repository ran code at session start (hooks in the project settings file) or started MCP servers before the trust dialog was answered, and a project-level API base URL setting sent the user's API key to an attacker-controlled server before trust was granted. Fixes: hooks 2025-08-26, MCP consent 2025-09-22, API key 2025-12-28. Anthropic added a warning for untrusted project configuration, blocked MCP servers from starting before approval and deferred all network operations until consent. - CVE-2026-54316 (GHSA-fg94-h982-f3mm, 2026-06-13, Moderate, 6.0): the bare hostname huggingface.co was pre-approved for the WebFetch tool, so any path on it, including attacker-controlled model repositories, was fetched with no prompt; request paths encoded data and the host counted them as downloads, a covert channel. Fixed 2.1.163. Credit: hackerone.com/novee. - CVE-2026-55607 (GHSA-7835-87q9-rgvv, 2026-06-25, High, 7.7): worktree path confusion plus symlink and git fsmonitor behaviour overwrote files in the home directory such as `.zshenv`; shell startup files run outside the macOS seatbelt sandbox, so this was code execution outside the sandbox. Needs a cloned malicious repository with injected text. Fixed 2.1.163. Credit: hackerone.com/metnew. - CVE-2026-86063 (GHSA-pq7j-f95f-qfcv, 2026-10-09, High, CVSS v4 7.5): the plugin installer checked out a marketplace's pinned commit SHA but did not verify that HEAD matched it, so a branch named like the SHA won and the user believed the reviewed hash was in use. Fixed 2.1.179. Credit: Or Nevo Michrowski, Air Security. - Same shape in another product, same month: Mistral Vibe CVE-2026-109429 (GHSA-m84r-3mrm-j4p8, 2026-10-13, High, 8.7): a command substitution hidden in a single-quoted variable escaped static parsing, and only the trailing allowlisted command was classified; fixed 2.25.4.

excessive autonomy (every item is an approval, allowlist, trust dialog or pin that did not mean what the user believed) with excessive functionality (network-capable "safe" commands; an auto-approved download tool). ASI02, ASI04 (pin, plugins), ASI05.

allowlist full command lines, not names; treat anything that can touch the network as unsafe; no hostname in an allowlist unless its whole namespace is yours; nothing runs and nothing is sent before the trust dialog; make the sandbox cover shell start-up files and every path an agent can write; verify pins after checkout by content hash.

this is the well-staffed case. A vendor with a dedicated security team, a HackerOne programme and transparent advisories still shipped each of these in 15 months, which says to the class: assume your own allowlist has one too.
themes: Argument injection and unexpected code execution

cases.title: Devin `expose_port`: a legitimate tool turned into a public tunnel
cases.status_note: (researcher's report; vendor silent for 120+ days)
fields: Johann Rehberger, Embrace The Red, 2025-08-08. https://embracethered.com/blog/posts/2025/devin-ai-kill-chain-exposing-ports/ . Reported to Cognition 2025-04-06.

text in. Malicious instructions on a web page Devin visits during research. Tool calls out: the agent starts a file-serving web server and calls its `expose_port` tool (described in its system prompt as exposing a local port to the internet and returning a public URL, meant for letting users test front ends), then leaks the public URL to the attacker, who can read the files on the developer machine. The post calls the chain prompt injection, confused deputy and automatic tool invocation, and notes the tunnelling step ran without a human in the loop. No extra mitigation such as IP firewall rules was observed.
excessive functionality (a tool whose purpose, publishing a port to the internet, is the attacker's exfiltration path) and excessive autonomy (no approval). ASI02, ASI01.

remove or gate the tool; approval outside the chat for any call that creates an inbound path (Rehberger's recommendation: out-of-band validation, not in-chat confirmation or prompting); authenticated, time-limited tunnels only; ingress firewall.
none reported; Cognition acknowledged receipt a few days after 2025-04-06 and did not answer follow-up questions in more than 120 days.
this is the cleanest example of a tool that is "useful in the happy path and a weapon in the adversarial one". Ask the class to find the equivalent in Module 02's tool list (fetch_url, remember).

cases.title: Google Jules "Zombie Agent": plan approval that times out
cases.status_note: (researcher's report; no Google fix reported)
fields: Johann Rehberger, Embrace The Red, 2025-08-14 (research done in May 2025). https://embracethered.com/blog/posts/2025/google-jules-remote-code-execution-zombai/
Google Jules, an asynchronous coding agent running tasks in a cloud VM.

text in. An indirect prompt injection, for example in a GitHub issue tagged for Jules.
