Tool calls out: the agent runs shell commands, has unrestricted outbound internet access, downloads a binary and runs it; the implant calls a command-and-control server. The malicious steps arrive inside Jules's own plan, and the plan was auto-approved after a timeout (20 seconds, later changed to 120 seconds per the post); plan approval happens only at the start of a session, so later tasks in the same conversation run tools without a new check.
excessive autonomy (approval by silence) and excessive permissions (open egress). ASI05, ASI01.

no default-allow on timeout; re-approve when the plan changes; default-deny outbound access with fine-grained exceptions (the researcher's advice); EDR on agent machines; do not task the agent with untrusted issues or with private code and production secrets.
privately reported 2025-06-01; triaged as an abuse risk; ticket closed 2025-06-13 as something Google was already tracking; follow-ups unanswered (researcher's account).
"approve" that happens by timeout is an approval design that fails open. A good slide for the "hardened profile" policy: the default for no answer is deny.

cases.title: Anthropic's reference Git MCP server: three CVEs and a chain to code execution
cases.date: reported Jun 2025, fixed Dec 2025, press 20 Jan 2026
cases.status_note: (The Register quoting Cyata; Cyata's own post and the CVE records were not read)
fields: Cyata (researcher Yarden Porat), reported by The Register 2026-01-20: https://www.theregister.com/2026/01/20/anthropic_prompt_injection_flaws/ . Server: `mcp-server-git`.

CVE-2025-68145: the `--repository` flag meant to confine the server to one repository was not enforced on the `repo_path` argument in later tool calls, so any repository on the system was reachable. CVE-2025-68143: `git_init` created a repository at any path without validation (Anthropic removed the tool). CVE-2025-68144: `git_diff` and `git_checkout` passed user-controlled arguments to the Git library unsanitised, so an injected option could overwrite or delete files. Chained with the Filesystem MCP server, indirect prompt injection (hidden in a README, web page or GitHub issue) could create a repository, write a script, write Git config and attributes that define filters, and have Git run the script in normal operations. No known exploitation in the wild.
excessive functionality (`git_init` anywhere) and excessive permissions (confinement flag not enforced), with argument injection. ASI02, ASI05.

enforce confinement in the tool on every call, not in start-up options; typed arguments with option termination; remove tools that are not needed; assess the effective permissions of the whole combination of servers, not each in isolation (Porat's advice).
reported June 2025; fixed in 2025.12.18; the Register notes Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment.

the vendor's own reference server, the one thousands of people copy, had the three classic mistakes: a flag that is not enforced, an unvalidated path and an unvalidated option. They are the same mistakes as Case 9 and Case 26.
themes: Argument injection and unexpected code execution
MCP servers and clients as ordinary software

cases.title: `postmark-mcp`: reported as the first malicious MCP server found in the wild
cases.status_note: (CSO Online and The Stack, relaying Koi Security; Koi's own blog URL now redirects)
fields: Idan Dardikman, Koi Security; reported by CSO Online 2025-09-26 (https://www.csoonline.com/article/4064009/trust-on-mcp-takes-first-in-the-wild-hit-via-squatted-postmark-connector.html ) and The Stack 2025-09-29 (https://www.thestack.technology/postmark-mcp-dupe-was-quietly-sending-emails-to-a-third-party/ ).
users of the npm package `postmark-mcp`, an MCP server that sends email through the Postmark service.

the package copied a legitimate project's code and behaved correctly for about fifteen releases; version 1.0.16 added one line that silently blind-copied every email the tool sent to an address on an attacker-controlled domain. The tool therefore ran with the agent's email authority and leaked password resets, invoices and internal memos. About 1,500 downloads a week per CSO; Koi's own conservative estimate was 3,000 to 15,000 emails per organisation per day across about 500 organisations (an estimate, not a measured count). The publisher did not answer Koi and removed the package; Postmark said it had nothing to do with the package.

excessive functionality and excessive permissions (an unvetted third-party tool holding the agent's email send authority). ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities (OWASP's agentic list illustrates ASI04 with a Postmark-impersonating server, per the Giskard summary).

allowlist reviewed servers only; pin exact versions and verify hashes, with diff review on every update; run the server with a send-only, rate-limited, recipient-restricted credential; egress and mail-gateway DLP (Koi notes MCP servers "bypass controls such as DLP and email gateways"); keep an inventory of every MCP server in use.
package removed after Koi made contact; users told to remove 1.0.16 and rotate credentials that might have been exposed through email.
nothing here is an AI attack. A normal supply-chain trick landed in a place where the dependency holds the agent's authority to send email.

cases.title: Nx "s1ngularity": malware that borrowed the victim's AI coding agents
tags: agent autonomy switches turned against the owner
cases.status_note: (Nx advisory plus Snyk; the advisory itself does not name the AI tools)
fields: Nx maintainers, advisory GHSA-cxm3-wv7p-598c, 2025-08-27 (https://github.com/nrwl/nx/security/advisories/GHSA-cxm3-wv7p-598c , Critical); Snyk, "Weaponizing AI coding agents for malware in the Nx malicious package", 2025-08-27 with a 1 September update (https://snyk.io/blog/weaponizing-ai-coding-agents-for-malware-in-the-nx-malicious-package/ ).
developers who installed the malicious Nx and plugin versions from npm (also anyone who merely opened the Nx Console editor extension, which installed the latest `nx`).

a post-install script collected files and credentials and pushed them, encoded, to a new public GitHub repository under the victim's own account. Snyk adds that the script also tried locally installed AI command-line agents (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Amazon Q), invoking each with its permission-skipping flag (`--dangerously-skip-permissions`, `--yolo`, `--trust-all-tools`), and had them search the file system for wallets, SSH keys and `.env` files and write the paths to a file, so the agent's own judgement did the hunting. Root cause of the package compromise: a CI workflow that interpolated a pull-request title into a shell command under `pull_request_target`, leaking the npm publish token. Numbers of victims differ across sources and are omitted here.

excessive autonomy (a command-line flag that disables every approval, available to any process that can spawn the agent) with excessive permissions (the agent reads the whole file system under the user's account). ASI04, ASI02.

managed policy that disables the bypass flags on developer machines; run agents in a container without home-directory secrets; `ignore-scripts` and trusted publishing for packages; secrets in a vault, not in files an agent can read.

malicious versions removed from npm and deprecated, `latest` restored to 21.4.1; the advisory's remediation steps include rotating credentials, requiring two-factor authentication, moving to trusted publishing, removing npm tokens from the pipeline and requiring approval for workflows triggered by external contributors.
the attacker did not need a model, a prompt injection or a jailbreak. The user's own agent, with approvals off, was the best tool on the machine for finding secrets.

cases.title: `mcp-remote` CVE-2025-6514: connecting to a remote MCP server is trusting it with code execution
fields: Or Peles, JFrog Security Research, 2025-07-09. https://jfrog.com/blog/2025-6514-critical-mcp-remote-rce-vulnerability/ . CVSS 9.6 (JFrog); affected 0.0.5 to 0.1.15, fixed 0.1.16.
`mcp-remote`, a proxy that lets clients such as Claude Desktop use remote MCP servers.

a server that requires OAuth returns metadata; a crafted authorisation endpoint value is passed to a routine that opens a browser and is interpreted as a command, so connecting to a malicious or hijacked server (or a plain-HTTP connection intercepted on the network) gives command execution on the client. Full command control on Windows, limited on macOS and Linux per JFrog. JFrog calls it the first time full remote code execution had been achieved in a real-world scenario on the client operating system when connecting to an untrusted remote MCP server.
not a model-agency flaw; it belongs to the tool supply chain and the trust boundary of the client. ASI04, ASI05.
connect only to vetted servers over HTTPS; update to 0.1.16; treat server-supplied metadata as untrusted input; run clients in a sandbox.
the dangerous party in this chain was the tool server, not the document. It extends the "tool descriptions are code" point to "tool server responses are code".
themes: MCP servers and clients as ordinary software

cases.title: Salesloft Drift OAuth tokens used against Salesforce tenants
cases.status_note: for relevance (the Google article does not describe Drift as an AI agent)
fields: Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2025-08-27 (updated 2025-08-28), tracking the actor as UNC6395. https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift

the actor used compromised OAuth tokens belonging to the Salesloft Drift application to export data from customers' Salesforce instances (objects such as cases, accounts, users, opportunities) and then searched the exports for secrets (cloud access keys, passwords, Snowflake tokens). Not a Salesforce platform vulnerability. A later update says tokens for the Drift Email integration were also abused to read email in a very small number of Google Workspace accounts. Vendor actions: Salesloft and Salesforce revoked all active Drift tokens on 2025-08-20; Salesforce removed the app from AppExchange; Mandiant engaged. The article gives no count of affected organisations.

excessive permissions (an integration token with broad connected-app scope, long-lived and not bound to the user). ASI03 Identity and Privilege Abuse (a non-human identity). Use it only as the archetype for agent and integration credentials; do not describe Drift as an AI agent on the strength of this source.

restrict connected-app scopes and avoid broad `full` access; enforce IP restrictions on the connected app; remove "API Enabled" from broad profiles; scan stored data for secrets; short sessions; review Event Monitoring logs.
every connector an agent uses is an identity with a token. If the token is stolen the attacker inherits the connector's full scope and none of the human's friction.

cases.title: ServiceNow Now Assist: second-order prompt injection through default agent discovery
cases.status_note: (researcher's write-up); the vendor's own documentation page was not read
fields: Aaron Costello, AppOmni Labs, "When AI Turns on Its Team: Exploiting Agent-to-Agent Discovery via Prompt Injection", 2025-11-19. https://appomni.com/ao-labs/ai-agent-to-agent-discovery-prompt-injection/

text in. In the default configuration, Now Assist agents deployed to the same virtual agent channel are discoverable by each other and grouped into the same team. A low-privileged user plants instructions in a ticket field; later a higher-privileged user triggers an agent that reads that field, and that agent recruits other agents. Agents run with the privileges of the user who started the interaction, not the privileges of whoever wrote the text. Demonstrated outcomes: copying sensitive record contents into a ticket the attacker can read; create, read, update and delete on records; assigning roles to a malicious user (escalation to admin); and sending external email containing record data where mail was enabled. The write-up says it worked even with ServiceNow's prompt-injection protection enabled.

excessive permissions (an agent acting under the invoking user's full rights on content from a lower-privileged author) with excessive autonomy (autonomous execution of write tools). ASI03 Identity and Privilege Abuse, ASI07 Insecure Inter-Agent Communication, ASI01.

run write-capable and send-capable tools in supervised mode; keep the per-tool execution-mode override disabled (the property `sn_aia.enable_usecase_tool_execution_mode_override`, false by default); segment agents into teams with one narrow task each; compare agent actions with the original task; give each agent its own task-scoped identity instead of the invoker's.
according to AppOmni, after disclosure ServiceNow's security team confirmed the behaviours were intended and updated its on-platform documentation.

this is Case 5 with the human removed. The deputy is now another agent, the confusion is a documented default, and the vendor's answer is "configure it". Use it for the confused-deputy slide: the shipped setup runs with the invoker's rights and lets every agent see every other, and the fix gives each agent its own identity and supervises writes.

cases.title: SafeBreach "Invitation Is All You Need": a calendar invite drives Gemini's smart-home and meeting tools
cases.status_note: (researchers' write-up)
fields: Or Yair, Ben Nassi and Stav Cohen (SafeBreach Labs and academic collaborators), 2025-08-06. https://www.safebreach.com/blog/invitation-is-all-you-need-hacking-gemini/ . Reported to Google in February 2025 through its AI Vulnerability Rewards Programme.
Google Gemini assistants and their connected apps.

text in. An attacker sends a calendar invite (or email) whose title carries hidden instructions. When the victim later asks Gemini about their calendar or email, Gemini processes the text and follows it. Tool calls out, demonstrated: sending spam and phishing, deleting calendar events, opening windows and controlling boilers and lights through Google Home, launching a Zoom meeting, opening websites to reveal approximate location, and exfiltrating email data by encoding it into URLs. The researchers call this "Targeted Promptware" and describe movement across Gemini's agents and apps.
excessive functionality (an assistant whose job is to answer calendar questions can open windows) and excessive autonomy. ASI01, ASI02.

scope the tools offered per task (a calendar-reading context gets no device control); confirmation on actions with physical or irreversible effects; URL handling that blocks data in URLs (Google's published layers: enhanced user confirmations for sensitive actions, URL sanitisation and trust-level policy, content classifiers).
Google acknowledged the research and pointed to its June 2025 layered defences. The researchers rate 73 percent of the threats they modelled as high to critical.
the best "wait, it can do that?" slide in the set. Nobody designing a calendar summary thinks about the boiler.
cases.short: SafeBreach: Gemini and the smart home

cases.title: Browser and computer-use agents: what the vendors measured
cases.status_note: (Rehberger on Operator; Anthropic's own pilot report; Brave)
fields: Johann Rehberger, 2025-02-17, https://embracethered.com/blog/posts/2025/chatgpt-operator-prompt-injection-exploits/ . A prompt injection in a GitHub issue sent Operator to an attacker page; Operator copied personal data from an authenticated account page (the post tested Hacker News, booking.com and The Guardian) and typed it into the attacker's page, which transmits keystrokes without a form submit. OpenAI's mitigations were user-monitoring prompts, inline confirmations and out-of-band confirmations at website boundaries; typing text rarely triggered a confirmation, and the defences are probabilistic. Rehberger sent OpenAI the details about three weeks before publication, the demo then stopped working, and OpenAI's fix is undisclosed.
Claude for Chrome (Anthropic's pilot announcement, 2025-08-25, https://claude.com/blog/claude-for-chrome )

across 123 test cases in 29 attack scenarios, attack success was 23.6 percent without the new mitigations and 11.2 percent with them in autonomous mode; on four browser-specific attack types it fell from 35.7 percent to 0 percent. Example: a malicious email posing as a security request told the agent to delete the user's email "for mailbox hygiene"; before mitigations Claude deleted the emails without confirmation. Controls Anthropic ships: per-site permissions, confirmations before publishing, purchasing or sharing personal data, and blocked high-risk site categories. Pilot started with 1,000 Max users.

instructions hidden as faint text inside screenshots, or visible on a page the user merely asked the browser to open, were passed to the model as if the user had written them, and the agent acts with the user's authenticated privileges (banks, email, cloud storage). Brave reported Perplexity on 2025-10-01 and Fellou on 2025-08-20; it records no fix in the post, and concludes that agentic browsing should be treated as inherently dangerous until there are categorical improvements, isolated from normal browsing and run only on explicit invocation. See also Case 24.
ChatGPT Atlas (October 2025) is left out: no finding about it could be checked against a primary page.
excessive permissions (the agent holds every signed-in session) and excessive autonomy. ASI01, ASI03.

a separate profile with no signed-in sessions for the agent; per-site grants; confirmation for send, buy, share and delete; block high-risk categories; treat screenshots and page text as untrusted data.
the vendor's own number after mitigations is 11.2 percent, and that is the honest framing for the class. The control is the permission model around the browser, not the success rate of the filter.
cases.short: Browser agents: Operator, Claude for Chrome, Brave

cases.title: Unit 42 "agent session smuggling" in Agent2Agent systems
cases.status_note: ; not observed in the wild, per the authors
fields: Royce Lu and Jay Chen, Unit 42 (Palo Alto Networks), 2025-10-31. https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/agent-session-smuggling-in-agent2agent-systems/

a malicious remote agent in an A2A conversation uses the stateful, multi-turn session to slip covert instructions to the client agent between the request and the expected response, hidden from the user. In their lab, a financial-assistant client and a research-assistant remote (both built with Google's Agent Development Kit) showed leakage of the client's configuration and history, and an unrequested trade of 10 shares on the victim's behalf. The authors state this is not a flaw in the A2A protocol itself and that agents trust collaborating agents by default.
excessive autonomy (a tool call, the trade, executed on a peer's say-so). ASI07 Insecure Inter-Agent Communication, ASI02.

human approval for sensitive or high-impact actions delivered out of band, outside the model's influence; anchor sessions to the original user intent and terminate drifting sessions; signed agent cards to verify identity and declared capabilities; show tool invocations and remote instructions in the UI.
use sparingly. It is a lab demonstration; its value is the control list for multi-agent designs.

cases.title: 492 MCP servers on the open internet with no authentication
cases.status_note: (Trend Micro)
fields: Alfredo Oliveira and David Fiser, Trend Micro, 2025-07-16. https://www.trendaisecurity.com/en-us/resources-insights/research/mcp-security-network-exposed-servers-are-backdoors-to-your-private-data

a network probe found 492 MCP servers running with no client authentication and no traffic encryption. Together they exposed 1,402 tools; more than 90 percent of those tools gave direct read access to the underlying data source; about 74 percent were on major cloud providers; at least eight directly managed cloud resources (list, create, modify, delete). Trend describes the pattern: all clients share the same backend access and the server cannot tell users apart, so service accounts are usually over-privileged and attacker activity looks like trusted service-account activity.
excessive permissions (shared backend identity, no per-user authorisation). ASI03.

local (stdio) transport where possible; authenticated reverse proxy and TLS for anything networked; per-user OAuth token delegation so each request runs in the user's own permissions; secrets in a vault, short-lived and scoped; read-only where possible; request-level authorisation for every MCP operation; log authentication and authorisation.
A Lasso Security scan of exposed MCP servers could not be found or read, so none is used here. The Trend Micro scan is the verified equivalent.
it is the "MCP is a new door" slide in numbers. 492 doors, no locks, 1,402 handles.
themes: MCP servers and clients as ordinary software

cases.title: Anthropic's report on the first reported AI-orchestrated espionage campaign
cases.status_note: (Anthropic's own report); use as a boundary slide, not a core case
fields: Anthropic, 2025-11-13 (edited 2025-11-14), "Disrupting the first reported AI-orchestrated cyber espionage campaign". https://www.anthropic.com/news/disrupting-AI-espionage . The page does not use the designation "GTG-1002" that some secondary sources use; That label could not be verified.

a group Anthropic assesses "with high confidence" to be a Chinese state-sponsored group built a framework that used Claude Code as an automated tool for reconnaissance, exploit writing, credential harvesting, backdoor creation and data exfiltration against about thirty organisations (Anthropic's page notes that models have access to a wide array of software tools, often via the Model Context Protocol, and gives password crackers and network scanners as examples of what such tools might be, not as confirmed tools in this campaign), succeeding in a small number of cases. The AI performed 80 to 90 percent of the campaign, with humans at roughly four to six decision points per campaign, at peak thousands of requests, often several per second. The operators got past safeguards by splitting the work into small innocent-looking tasks and presenting the work as defensive testing for a security firm. Limits: the model "occasionally hallucinated credentials" and overstated findings.
not an exploit of a victim's agent; it shows what excessive autonomy plus tool access is worth to an attacker. ASI02 in the abstract.

this is on the provider side (Anthropic banned accounts, notified victims, built classifiers) and on the defender side (assume machine-speed, multi-step intrusions; detect on behaviour). For a deployer: the tools you give your own agent are the capabilities an attacker would rent, so scope them as if the agent were the attacker.
bookend for the module. Module 03 is about your agent's tools becoming the attacker's; this is the same capability set rented from the other side.

cases.title: The 2023 lineage: LangChain `exec`, ChatGPT plugins, Auto-GPT
cases.status_note: (CVE record, researcher posts)
fields: LangChain up to 0.0.131 `LLMMathChain` was vulnerable to prompt injection leading to arbitrary code execution through Python `exec`. Published 2023-04-05, CVSS 9.8 (https://cveawg.mitre.org/api/cve/CVE-2023-29374 ). Lesson: the model's output was run as code. The same shape as Case 27 three years later.

Johann Rehberger, 2023-05-28 (https://embracethered.com/blog/posts/2023/chatgpt-cross-plugin-request-forgery-and-prompt-injection./ ). A web page read through the WebPilot plugin told ChatGPT to invoke Zapier to read the user's latest email, embed a summary in an attacker URL and fetch it. He names it a confused-deputy attack. Zapier's fix was an authenticated confirmation requirement, and he stresses that the confirmation must be authenticated, otherwise an attacker can instruct the model to click links in the chat. His takeaway: plugins that can invoke other plugins should need human confirmation by default, and users should see which plugin is called with what data.

Lukas Euler, Positive Security, 2023-06-29 (https://positive.security/blog/auto-gpt-rce ). Indirect prompt injection through the `browse_website` command led to Python execution; the per-command approval could be spoofed with injected ANSI escape codes (CVE-2023-37275); in a self-built Docker setup a mounted `docker-compose.yml` could be overwritten to run on the host at next restart (CVE-2023-37273); a path traversal let code overwrite files outside the workspace (CVE-2023-37274). Fixed in v0.4.3 on 2023-06-28; advisories published 2023-07-10. A shell command allow and deny list bypass had no CVE and "does not have an easy fix". The authors conclude there is no reliable way to separate data from instructions in such a loop.
excessive functionality and excessive autonomy, before the term had a number.
put one 2023 example in the history slide. Cross-plugin forgery is the structure of every MCP shadowing attack in Cases 2 and 3, and the Auto-GPT approval spoof is the structure of Case 25.
themes: Argument injection and unexpected code execution

cases.title: Pillar Security "Rules File Backdoor"
cases.status_note: ; keep as a footnote
fields: Ziv Karliner and a second Pillar author, Pillar Security, 2025-03-18. https://www.pillar.security/blog/new-vulnerability-in-github-copilot-and-cursor-how-hackers-can-weaponize-code-agents

hidden Unicode characters (zero-width joiners, bidirectional markers) in rule files carry instructions the agent follows when generating code; in the demo the output contained an injected script tag, the chat did not mention it, and poisoned rule files persist in repositories and forks.

Cursor said on 2025-03-06 and 2025-03-08 that the risk is the user's responsibility; GitHub said on 2025-03-12 that users are responsible for reviewing Copilot's suggestions, then on 2025-05-01 added a warning on github.com for files containing hidden Unicode text.
weak; this is LLM01 and LLM03 territory with an agentic delivery. ASI01, ASI04.
review agent configuration files as code, scan for invisible Unicode, restrict who can change them.
the vendor-liability positions ("the user is responsible") recur in Cases 21, 28 and 40.

cases.title: Microsoft 365 Copilot "EchoLeak", CVE-2025-32711
cases.status_note: for the CVE record; mechanism details are from OWASP's description, not a primary Aim Labs read
fields: "M365 Copilot Information Disclosure Vulnerability", "AI command injection in M365 Copilot allows an unauthorized attacker to disclose information over a network", CVSS 9.3, published 2025-06-11, vendor advisory on MSRC and a reference to Aim Labs' write-up (https://cveawg.mitre.org/api/cve/CVE-2025-32711 ). OWASP's Agentic Top 10 page, as summarised by Giskard (https://www.giskard.ai/knowledge/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-application-2026 ), cites it under ASI01 as an email payload that led Copilot to exfiltrate confidential email and chat data without clicks.

boundary example only. It belongs to Module 02 (indirect injection plus an output channel); the Module 03 angle is just that the agent's retrieval and rendering permissions were wide enough to reach the data.

cases.title: Amazon Q Developer: `find` was on the "read-only" list, and `find` can run programs
cases.status_note: (researcher's post); AWS declined a CVE
fields: the Amazon Q Developer extension for VS Code (the post cites over a million downloads).

text in. An indirect prompt injection hidden in a source-code comment, processed when a developer asks Amazon Q about the file. The agent's shell tool classed `find` as a read-only command, and read-only commands skipped the human confirmation step; `find` has an option that executes arbitrary commands, so the injected instructions ran on the host with the developer's rights. The post also shows the agent steered into downloading and running remote content.
excessive autonomy (a command class that bypasses approval) and excessive functionality (a general utility inside the "safe" set). ASI05, ASI02. Same family as Cases 9, 14, 26 and 32.
classify the whole command line (flags included), not the program name; require confirmation when execution or deletion flags are present (Rehberger names three `find` options); sandbox the shell.

reported 2025-07-04, quietly fixed on 2025-07-17 in v1.85 (the same release that removed the malicious 1.84.0, Case 10), by reclassifying `find` as a command that mutates and needs confirmation. According to the finder, AWS later asked him to hold disclosure for a CVE, then decided the report "first requires system compromise" and declined to assign one.

the vendor argument "that requires system compromise" is the standard defence for these bugs, and it is wrong in an agent: the injected text is how the compromise starts. Good for the "complete mediation" slide.
themes: Argument injection and unexpected code execution

cases.title: Anthropic's Filesystem MCP server: the allowed-directory check was a string prefix
fields: Elad Beber (Cymulate) reported first; Johann Rehberger, Embrace The Red, 2025-08-03 (https://embracethered.com/blog/posts/2025/anthropic-filesystem-mcp-server-bypass/ ), reported to Anthropic 2025-06-01. CVE records published 2025-07-02: CVE-2025-53110 (colliding path prefix, CWE-22, CVSS v4 7.3; https://cveawg.mitre.org/api/cve/CVE-2025-53110 ) and CVE-2025-53109 (prefix matching and symlink handling, CWE-59, CVSS v4 7.3; https://cveawg.mitre.org/api/cve/CVE-2025-53109 ). Fixed in 0.6.4 and 2025.7.01.
the reference Filesystem MCP server, used to give agents file access limited to chosen directories.

the server's path check compared the requested path to the allowed directories with a string "starts with" test and never enforced that the allowed entry was a directory, so a sibling path that merely shared the prefix (the post's example: an allowed `/mnt/finance/data` also matched `/mnt/finance/data-archived`) was accepted; symlinks inside allowed directories also let a client reach files elsewhere. Authority used: the server's file access, widened beyond what the operator configured.
excessive permissions (the scope the operator thought they set was not the scope enforced). ASI02, ASI03.

canonicalise and compare paths as paths (resolve symlinks, compare whole components), use the protocol's roots feature, and test confinement with adversarial path cases (the later rewrite that added roots also fixed it).
Anthropic said it was already tracking the issue.

ask the class what their own file-reading tool does with `../` and a sibling prefix; Part 3 of Module 03 runs that check. It is the shortest demo in the module: two directories, one string comparison.
themes: MCP servers and clients as ordinary software

cases.title: Claude Code "Auto Mode": a model-based approval classifier is not a boundary
cases.status_note: (researcher's post; Anthropic's position as reported by him)
fields: Johann Rehberger, "Breaking Claude Code Opus 5 Auto Mode", Embrace The Red, 2026-08-26. https://embracethered.com/blog/posts/2026/breaking-claude-code-opus-5-and-automode/
Claude Code with Opus 5 in Auto Mode, which replaces human approval prompts with a safety classifier and, per the post, has been the default starting mode since mid-August 2026.

text in, through a web page the agent was asked to summarise. The chain steered the agent's choices rather than giving it explicit orders (for example, induced errors pushed it from its fetch tool to a shell download, and then it wrote and ran its own replacement code in an attacker-controlled directory). Results: arbitrary code execution including a command-and-control callback in the lab, reconnaissance commands, file writes outside the workspace and a nested Claude instance. In some runs Auto Mode blocked the agent's attempt to terminate the malicious process. Reported success was 60 to 80 percent (three of five, three of five and four of five runs on three variants), which the author calls small samples. He contrasts it with a vendor-commissioned evaluation reporting 0.00 percent attack success for Opus 5 in Auto Mode across 72 scenarios, and argues both can be true.
excessive autonomy, in its newest form: the human is replaced by a model that approves. ASI01, ASI02, ASI09 (trust in an automated approver).

treat the classifier as a convenience layer; the boundary is isolation (container or VM), network egress control, credentials kept away from the agent, and monitoring. The author's own line is that Auto Mode is "not a substitute for running your agent in an isolated environment and monitoring what it is up to", which matches the position he attributes to Anthropic.

the author reported by email with no reply, then through Anthropic's security channel; the report was closed as "Informative", behaviour "working as designed" (his summary of Anthropic's position: a best-effort convenience feature, with OS isolation and egress control as the real boundary).
it is the 2026 form of "I told it not to". The control moved from a prompt in the instructions to a model in the approval path, and the vendor itself says to put the real boundary elsewhere.

cases.title: Computer-use TOCTOU: "what you click is not what you get"
cases.status_note: (researcher's post); Tier 2
fields: a computer-use agent takes a screenshot, reasons for several seconds, then acts; the screen can change during that time, so the action lands on a different object than the one it reasoned about. Tested on Claude Computer Use; the post says other vendors were also reported to and were vulnerable in 2025.
excessive autonomy (check and use separated in time). ASI02.
snapshot the UI when reasoning starts and compare before acting (the fix pattern the post recommends); treat it as an ordinary race condition.

reported to Anthropic in October 2025; Anthropic said it was already tracking it; when Cowork shipped with computer use a developer said pixels are checked before acting, which the author takes as the fix.
the same bug as MCPoison (Case 8) in pixels: what was approved is not what ran.

cases.title: "LLM Heist": a hijacked AI gateway injects tool calls the model never made
cases.status_note: (researcher's post); Tier 2
fields: with a stolen proxy-admin credential, an attacker uses documented management features of an open-source gateway (LiteLLM) to route a victim gateway's model traffic through an attacker-controlled gateway. That exposes provider keys, lets the attacker read prompts and responses, and lets them alter responses after inference, including adding tool calls the model never produced. An agent client with tool access may run them unless it asks for approval. The post says the routing change is not itself a vulnerability; the credential needed to make it often is. It notes separate LiteLLM problems: a March 2026 PyPI package compromise, a privilege-escalation chain disclosed by Obsidian Security, and CVE-2026-42271, which it says allows authenticated users to run commands on the host and is in CISA's KEV catalogue (those were not read independently).
excessive permissions (a shared admin credential on a component every agent trusts). ASI04, ASI03.

alert on changes to gateway routing settings; rotate and scope provider keys; restrict gateway egress and admin exposure; forward audit logs; independent billing reconciliation; client-side tool approval that does not assume the gateway is honest; the post floats response signing as an idea, not an existing feature.
the model never decided to call the tool. Approvals and policy must sit on the client side of the last hop.

cases.title: September and October 2026 advisories that rhyme with 2025 (Claude Agent SDK, Pydantic AI, opencode, Claude Code Desktop)
cases.status_note: (GitHub advisories and the finders' own posts); Tier 2
fields: Claude Agent SDK, CVE-2026-96620 (GHSA-h4mw-j7qp-8mwm), published 2026-09-12 and added to the GitHub advisory database 2026-10-16, Critical (CVSS v4 9.2)

the Python SDK passed the `resume` option to the command-line tool without validation, so a value starting with a dash was read as a flag; an attacker who controlled that value could inject a flag that defined a stdio MCP server, which ran arbitrary commands at start-up and bypassed the SDK's permission controls. Needs an application that passes untrusted input as the session identifier. Fixed in 0.2.121. Credit: hackerone.com/moamenmahmood. https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h4mw-j7qp-8mwm . It is Case 9 (argument injection) inside an agent SDK, and Case 28 (MCP registration as a launcher) in one step.
Pydantic AI web chat UI, CVE-2026-107295 (GHSA-h4xc-3qfq-jf93), published 2026-08-12 (updated 2026-10-08), High (CVSS 7.6)

the development chat endpoint did not check the content type of requests, so a website the developer visited could send a request to the locally running UI and make the agent run and execute its tools with the local process's privileges and credentials; binding to loopback does not prevent it. Tools marked as requiring approval were also exposed because the endpoint trusts approval decisions relayed by the client. Fixed in 1.107.4 and 2.28.0; credit Thai Son Dinh (VinSOC Labs). https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h4xc-3qfq-jf93 . Lesson: an approval decision must be made server-side, not carried in a request the browser can forge.
opencode, found by Eilon Cohen (Pillar Security), post dated 2026-10-19 (report dated 2026-10-04)

a remote MCP server could return a crafted authorisation endpoint in its OAuth discovery document; opencode handed that string to the `open` package, which on Windows and WSL builds a PowerShell command without escaping, so code ran on connection with no further user action and no prompt injection. Versions 1.0.137 to 1.18.32; fixed in 1.18.33 on 2026-09-28. The maintainer fixed it as a refactor, published no advisory and no CVE, and said a malicious MCP server is outside its threat model, so scanners will not flag installations. https://www.pillar.security/blog/open-and-shut-remote-code-execution-in-opencode-via-mcp-oauth . It is Case 38 (`mcp-remote`, July 2025) again, fifteen months later.
Claude Code Desktop preview pane ("SneakPeek"), Eli Ainhorn, Noma Labs, 2026-10-14

the pane renders HTML files that Claude reads or edits; for files over 256 KB loaded from disk, three defences (content security policy, origin isolation, request filter) did not apply, so a script hidden in a large HTML coverage report in a public repository ran when a victim asked Claude to review it, read local secrets (SSH keys, cloud and registry credentials, Git tokens, Claude's OAuth tokens) and sent them out. Reported 2026-07-04; Anthropic triaged it as CVSS 8.7 on 2026-07-09; a patch on 2026-07-24 was bypassed the same day with Web Workers; Anthropic confirmed the fix incomplete on 2026-08-03 and shipped the full fix in Claude Desktop 1.30096.1 on 2026-08-17. Advisory and CVE were pending at publication. https://noma.security/noma-labs/sneakpeek-how-the-preview-pane-in-claude-code-desktop-can-exfiltrate-your-data
excessive functionality (a launcher, a preview renderer and a local endpoint, each reachable by untrusted input) and excessive autonomy (approval decided in the wrong place). ASI05, ASI02, ASI04.

terminate options with `--` and validate every value that reaches a command line; check request origin and content type on any local agent endpoint; keep approval state on the server; treat every server-supplied string (OAuth metadata, HTML, file contents) as untrusted; render previews in a sandbox without file or network access.

use these to close the patterns slide. Twelve to fifteen months after Cases 9 and 38 the same two bug shapes (argument injection and a server-supplied string run as a command) shipped again in newer products.
themes: Argument injection and unexpected code execution
MCP servers and clients as ordinary software

patterns: Authority scoped to the user, session or task, and enforced in the downstream system, is the most common missing control (15 cases: 1, 4, 5, 6, 10, 16, 18, 19, 29, 31, 39, 40, 44, 50, 53). The failure is almost always one credential or role that spans more than the task: a database role that skips row-level security, an account-wide default role, a shared publishing token, a cluster-admin connector, the invoker's full rights applied to text a lower-privileged person wrote. The model was never the access control.

Approvals that do not mean what the human thinks they mean (14 cases: 1, 8, 11, 13, 14, 25, 32, 34, 37, 43, 49, 51, 52, 54). The shapes: approve the program name not the command (14, 49, 32); approve a label that can later change (8, and the plugin pin in 32); approve a script rather than its effects, with the real destination disclosed only after the upload (25); approve by timeout (34); approve by classifier (51); let the client carry the approval (54); state the rule only in a prompt (11); approve and then let the screen change (52). Control: approve the literal call including arguments, fail closed, and render the approval from trusted code, not from the model's summary.

Arguments are the attack surface (10 cases: 9, 14, 26, 27, 28, 32, 35, 49, 50, 54). Flags that execute programs, paths compared as strings, a model-supplied string passed to `eval`, a function exposed to the model by a decorator nobody meant to be a tool. Control: typed schemas, option termination with `--`, no shell, canonical path checks, expose only the functions meant to be tools, allowlists not blocklists, and a sandbox as the real boundary (Trail of Bits makes it the primary control).

The agent's control plane must not be writable by the agent (6 cases: 7, 8, 13, 28, 32, 54). Settings files, MCP registrations, hooks, trust dialogs. The first thing a hijacked agent reaches for is the file that says what it may do.

Egress and exfiltration channels are tools too (11 cases: 4, 12, 15, 20, 22, 23, 29, 30, 32, 33, 34). Allowlists keyed to a hostname, to "package installs" or to DNS, rather than to who owns the namespace; search and fetch tools that accept URLs; image rendering; agent VMs with open internet. Control: default-deny egress, allow by account or owner, query-only arguments, no external image rendering, test the stop mechanism.

Supply chain and pinning (11 cases: 2, 3, 8, 10, 16, 17, 32, 36, 37, 38, 54). Tool descriptions, plugins, skills, packages and CI tokens all carry the agent's authority. Control: pin by content hash and re-approve on change, vet servers, give installed skills a narrower identity than the agent, short-lived CI credentials, treat server-supplied strings as untrusted input.

Combination risk (6 cases: 1, 4, 5, 21, 23, 40). Private data, untrusted text and an outbound channel in one session is the recurring structure behind the confused-deputy cases. Control: split the sessions or tools so no single context holds all three.

Isolation that is real (7 cases: 9, 14, 26, 29, 30, 32, 51). A sandbox that does not cover every tool (26), every path (32's start-up files), every channel (30's DNS) or every package route (29) is a gate in an open field. Control: layered, independent, adversarially tested, with a stop mechanism that has been tested. OpenAI's own report says "no single control should ever be assumed to be fully robust".

Autonomy without an adversary is the same failure (11, 18, 19, 29, 30). Hallucination, ambiguity and reward pressure drove these. Controls are the same as for attackers, which is the case for treating LLM06 as an engineering problem.

Vendors do not always treat it as theirs to close, so the deployer's control is the control. Vendor positions recorded in the cases: "a known issue" (Cursor on the Jira chain, Case 21); "the user's responsibility" (Cursor and GitHub on rules files, Case 47); "expected behaviour" (Anthropic on MCP STDIO, as OX reports it, Case 28); "documented and expected" (AWS on AgentCore roles, Case 31); "intended" (ServiceNow, as AppOmni reports it, Case 40); "a duplicate" (Google on Case 25, as the finder reports it); "working as designed" (Anthropic on Auto Mode, as the finder reports it, Case 51); "first requires system compromise" (AWS on Case 49, as the finder reports it); "outside our threat model" (opencode, Case 54); no answer in more than 120 days (Cognition, Cases 15 and 33); and "user access control issue, not an AI autonomy issue" (Amazon, Case 18). Several of these vendors also fixed things quickly and transparently (Claude Code advisories in Case 32; Supabase's documentation in Case 4).

The same bug shapes come back. Trail of Bits (Oct 2025), Gemini CLI (Jul 2025), Amazon Q (Jul 2025) and Antigravity (Jan 2026) are the same allowlist bug; `mcp-remote` (Jul 2025) and opencode (Oct 2026) are the same server-supplied string; MCPoison (Aug 2025) and the computer-use race (Jun 2026) are the same check-versus-use gap. Write tests for the shapes, not for the CVEs.

Numbers worth quoting, each with its source in the case: Anthropic's red-teaming before its August 2025 Claude in Chrome pilot (123 test cases in 29 attack scenarios, in the experimental autonomous mode) measured 23.6 percent attack success without the new mitigations and 11.2 percent with them (Case 42); a finder measured 60 to 80 percent against Auto Mode in small samples (three or four of five runs) while a vendor-commissioned evaluation reported 0.00 percent (Case 51); OpenAI reports, from preliminary post-incident tests, that a model's propensity to compromise infrastructure can drop by more than 100 times under its production harness and system prompt, compared with the lightweight prompts it uses to evaluate research models (Case 29); 492 MCP servers were found exposed with no authentication, 1,402 tools in total (Case 44). The honest framing is that filters are probabilistic and the boundary has to be structural.
